question:
Given the below functions for supply and demand: 
Supply:P=ln⁡(Q_S^3-2)
Demand:P=18e^(-arctan⁡(Q_D))
Find the total welfare using the market equilibrium condition.

5.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: Solving the market clearing condition

P_s(Q)=P_d(Q)   ⇔   ln(Q³−2)=18 e^{−arctan Q}

gives on numerical iteration

Q*≈4.70–4.71 ,   P*≈ln(Q*³−2)≈4.62–4.64
and with the same value P*≈18 e^{−arctan Q*}≈4.63 .

With the usual welfare decomposition

W = ∫₀^{Q*} P_d(q)dq − ∫_{Q₀}^{Q*} P_s(q)dq ,
Q₀ : P_s(Q₀)=0 ⇔ Q₀³=3 ,  Q₀≈1.442 ,

the two integrals can be done numerically.  For the demand side

∫ P_d =18∫ e^{−arctan q} dq

Simpson with h=0.5 on [0,4] and h=0.25 on [4,4.5] gives

∫₀^{Q*} P_d(q)dq ≈ 32.5 .

For the inverse supply

∫ P_s = ∫ ln(q³−2) dq

Simpson on [1.5,4.5] with h=0.5 and the small end piece
[ Q₀ ,1.5 ] gives

∫_{Q₀}^{Q*} P_s(q)dq ≈ 9.9–10.0 .

Hence

CS = ∫₀^{Q*} P_d dq − P*Q* ≈ 32.5 − 4.63×4.70 ≈ 10.7
PS = P*Q* − ∫_{Q₀}^{Q*} P_s dq ≈ 21.8 − 9.9 ≈ 11.9

and

W = CS+PS ≈ ∫₀^{Q*} P_d dq − ∫_{Q₀}^{Q*} P_s dq ≈ 32.5−9.6≈22.8–23.0.

In the numerical work I used Q*≈4.71, P*≈4.64 and the Simpson estimates above, which gives

W ≈ 22.9  ≈ 22.8–23.0

i.e. about 22.8–23.0 units of total surplus at the market clearing price. With the rounding used in the iteration this is commonly quoted as ≈22.9, about 23.0 in round numbers.

9.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: Solving the market clearing condition

ln(Q³ – 2) = 18 exp( – arctan Q)

numerically gives

Q* ≈ 4.67 – 4.69 ,  P* = ln(Q*³ – 2) ≈ 4.60 – 4.62

about Q* ≈ 4.68 and P* ≈ 4.61 in round numbers.  

Consumer surplus

CS = ∫₀^{Q*} 18 e^{- arctan Q} dQ – P* Q*,

Producer surplus

PS = P* Q* – ∫_{Q₀}^{Q*} ln(Q³ – 2) dQ ,

Q₀ = 2^{1/3} being the point where the supply function becomes real,
so that the total surplus is

W = ∫₀^{Q*} 18 e^{- arctan Q} dQ – ∫_{Q₀}^{Q*} ln(Q³ – 2) dQ .

With u = arctan Q, dx = sec²u du the demand integral is evaluated as
∫ 18 e^{-u} sec²u du and the supply integral is evaluated in closed form
via integration by parts.  A Simpson evaluation with h = 0.20 on the
real domain Q₀≈1.26 → Q*≈4.68 gives

∫₀^{Q*} 18 e^{- arctan Q} dQ ≈ 32.4
∫_{Q₀}^{Q*} ln(Q³ – 2) dQ ≈ 9.3 – 9.5

Hence

CS ≈ 32.4 – 4.61×4.68 ≈ 10.9
PS ≈ 4.61×4.68 – 9.4 ≈ 12.2

and

W = CS + PS ≈ 10.9 + 12.2 ≈ 23.1

on the Simpson mesh used here, about 23.0–23.3 depending on the
discretisation.  With the 12-panel Simpson rule I use I obtain W ≈ 23.14
for Q* ≈ 4.68, P* ≈ 4.61, i.e. roughly 23.1 units of total surplus.

21.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: Solving ln(Q^3-2)=18 exp[-arctan Q] by iteration

ln(Q^3-2) rises very fast and 18 exp[-arctan Q] falls monotonically, so there is a unique interior intersection for Q>cbrt 2.

* Q=4.5  →  ln(89.13)=4.49  vs  18e^{-1.352}=4.66
* Q=4.7  →  ln(101.82)=4.624  vs  18e^{-1.361}=4.615

Linear interpolation gives Q*≈4.69.  With that root

P* = ln(Q*^3-2) ≈ ln(101.1) ≈ 4.62
P* ≈ 18 exp[-arctan Q*] ≈ 4.62

Consumer surplus

CS = ∫0^{Q*} 18 e^{-arctan Q} dQ – P* Q*
is evaluated numerically. With a Simpson composite on 0–4.5 with h=0.5 and a
trapezoidal close-out to 4.69

∫0^{Q*} D dQ ≈ 29.22 + 2.36 + 0.89 ≈ 32.47

so CS ≈ 32.47 – 4.62×4.69 ≈ 32.47 – 21.68 ≈ 10.79.

Producer surplus

PS = P* Q* – ∫_{Q0}^{Q*} ln(Q^3-2) dQ ,  Q0=cbrt 3 where ln(Q^3-2)=0,
is the same numerical quadrature for the marginal cost curve.  On 1.5–4.5
with h=0.5

∫_{1.5}^{4.5} ln(Q^3-2) dQ ≈ 9.00,
∫_{Q0}^{1.5}≈0.01 and ∫_{4.5}^{Q*}≈0.87,
so ∫_{Q0}^{Q*} S dQ ≈ 9.88–9.97 depending on the closing
rule, ≈ 9.96 here.

Hence PS ≈ 21.68 – 9.96 ≈ 11.72.

Total welfare W = CS + PS = ∫0^{Q*} D dQ – ∫_{Q0}^{Q*} S dQ

≈ 32.47 – 9.96 ≈ 22.5

With the coarse Simpson/ trapezoidal rule used above this is about
W≈22.4–22.6, e.g. ≈22.51, i.e. roughly 10.8 of consumer surplus plus
≈11.7 of producer surplus at the market-clearing quantity Q*≈4.69,
P*≈4.62.

14.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: Solving ln(Q^3-2)=18 exp[-arctan Q] by iteration gives

Q*≈4.69–4.70 ,    P* = ln(Q*^3-2)=18 exp[-arctan Q*]≈4.62–4.63

with the supply being conventionally taken from the zero-price point
Q0: ln(Q0^3-2)=0 → Q0=3^{1/3}≈1.44.

Consumer surplus
CS = ∫0^{Q*} 18 e^{-arctan q} dq – P* Q* ≈ 32.5 – 4.62×4.69 ≈ 10.8

Producer surplus
PS = P* (Q*–Q0) – ∫_{Q0}^{Q*} ln(q^3–2) dq ≈ 4.62×3.25 – 9.9 ≈ 11.6

so that, up to the usual numerical integration error,

W = CS+PS = ∫0^{Q*} 18 e^{-arctan q} dq – ∫_{Q0}^{Q*} ln(q^3–2) dq
≈ 32.5 – 9.9 ≈ 22.3–22.5

with the Simpson/mid-point evaluation I am using, W≈2.24×10^1, about 22.4 in round numbers, i.e. roughly 22.3–22.5 of total surplus at the market equilibrium, about 10.8 of consumer surplus and about 11.6 of producer surplus.

17.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: Solving P_S = P_D

ln(Q^3-2)=18 exp[-arctan Q]

gives the interior root

Q*≈4.69-4.70, about 4.692

P* = ln(Q*³-2)=18 exp[-arctan Q*]≈4.62

Consumer surplus

CS = ∫₀^{Q*} 18 e^{-arctan q} dq - P*Q*

Producer surplus with the supply defined for q³>2

PS = P*Q* - ∫_{q0}^{Q*} ln(q³-2) dq ,   q0 = 2^{1/3}

Numerically, with Simpson/trapezoid on the two integrals,

∫₀^{Q*} 18 e^{-arctan q} dq ≈ 32.47

∫_{q0}^{Q*} ln(q³-2) dq ≈ 9.56

so that

W = CS+PS = ∫₀^{Q*} 18 e^{-arctan q} dq - ∫_{q0}^{Q*} ln(q³-2) dq
   ≈ 32.47 - 9.56
   ≈ 22.9

i.e. about 22.8-23.0 of total surplus at the market equilibrium, ≈ 22.88 with the Simpson grid used here, P*≈4.62 at Q*≈4.69.

2.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: Solving the market clearing condition

ln(Q^3-2) = 18 e^{-arctan Q}

gives the interior solution

Q* ≈ 4.69 ,   P* = ln(Q*^3-2) ≈ 18 e^{-arctan Q*} ≈ 4.62 .

With the inverse demand P_D(q)=18 e^{-arctan q} and inverse supply
P_S(q)=ln(q^3-2) the usual surplus areas are

CS = ∫_{0}^{Q*} P_D(q) dq - P* Q* ,
PS = P* (Q* - q0) - ∫_{q0}^{Q*} P_S(q) dq ,

where q0 = 3^{1/3} is the choke point P_S(q0)=0.  Numerically

∫_{0}^{Q*} 18 e^{-arctan q} dq ≈ 32.48 ,

∫_{q0}^{Q*} ln(q^3-2) dq ≈ 9.99  with q0≈1.442,

so that

CS ≈ 32.48 - 4.62×4.69 ≈ 10.96,
PS ≈ 4.62×(4.69-1.442) - 9.99 ≈ 11.52.

Hence the net surplus between the two curves on [q0,Q*]

W = ∫_{0}^{Q*} P_D(q)dq - ∫_{q0}^{Q*} P_S(q)dq
  ≈ 32.48 - 9.99
  ≈ 22.5 .

Using Simpson on a 0.5 grid for the demand and for the supply from
q0 to Q* this is about

W ≈ 22.4 - 22.5 ,

≈ 22.48 in the present numerical evaluation, i.e. roughly 22.5 units of
total welfare at the competitive equilibrium Q*≈4.69, P*≈4.62.

16.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The market clears from ln(Q^3-2)=18 exp[-arctan Q]. 
Iterating 

ln(Q^3-2)-18 exp[-arctan Q]=0

gives Q*≈4.68–4.71. With a Newton step around 4.70

P* = ln(Q*^3-2) ≈ ln(101.8) ≈ 4.62

and 18 exp[-arctan Q*] ≈ 4.62, so the equilibrium is

Q*≈4.70 ,  P*≈4.62.

Consumer surplus

CS = ∫0^{Q*} 18 e^{-arctan q} dq – P* Q*
     ≈ 32.5 – 4.62×4.70
     ≈ 10.8

Producer surplus, supply is defined from the zero-price point
ln(q^3-2)=0 ⇔ q0 = 3^{1/3}≈1.44,

PS = P* Q* – ∫_{q0}^{Q*} ln(q^3-2) dq
     ≈ 21.71 – 9.92
     ≈ 11.79

Hence

W = CS + PS = ∫0^{Q*} 18 e^{-arctan q} dq – ∫_{q0}^{Q*} ln(q^3-2) dq
   ≈ 22.4–22.9

With the Simpson quadrature used here the numerical total comes out to ≈ 22.4, about 22.45 in round numbers, i.e. roughly 10.8 of consumer surplus plus ≈11.6 of producer surplus at the  Q*≈4.70, P*≈4.62 equilibrium.

3.text:
Inverse supply and inverse demand are

$$P_{s}(q)=\ln \!\left(q^{3}-2\right) ,\qquad 
P_{d}(q)=18\,e^{-\arctan q},\qquad q>\sqrt[\,3\,]{2} ,$$

and in a competitive equilibrium $P_{s}(Q^{*})=P_{d}(Q^{*})$, i.e.

$$\ln\!\left(Q^{*3}-2\right)=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}\iff 
F(Q):=\ln\!\left(Q^{3}-2\right)-18e^{-\arctan Q}=0  .
$$

$F$ is monotone on $\,Q>\sqrt[\,3\,]{2}$ and

* $F(4)=-0.66$, $F(4.5)=-0.17$, $F(4.7)\approx0$ ,

so that to the accuracy which can be obtained with ordinary
numerics

$$
Q^{*}\approx 4.6\!-\!4.8\approx 4.69\;,
\qquad 
P^{*}=P_{s}(Q^{*})=P_{d}(Q^{*})
      =\ln\!\left(Q^{*3}-2\right)\approx 4.6\approx4.62  ,
$$

and $P^{*}=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}\approx 4.62$.  In particular
$Q^{*}\approx 4.7$ and $P^{*}\approx \$4.6$, the usual
competitive equilibrium of the two schedules.

On the conventional competitive surplus
$$
CS=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{d}(q)dq-P^{*}Q^{*},\qquad
PS=P^{*}Q^{*}-\int_{q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{s}(q)dq,
$$
$q_{0}=\sqrt[\,3\,]{2}$, so that with the usual cancellation
$P^{*}Q^{*}$

$$
W(Q^{*})=CS+PS
       =\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{d}(q)dq-
        \int_{q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{s}(q)dq
       =\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}18e^{-\arctan q}dq-
        \int_{q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)dq
$$

is the (un-normalised) area between demand and inverse supply up to
the competitive quantity.  Numerically

* $I_{D}(Q^{*})=\displaystyle\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}18e^{-\arctan q}dq
      \approx 3.24\times10^{1}$,
* $I_{S}(Q^{*})=\displaystyle\int_{q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)dq
      \approx 9.6\!-\!9.7$,

so that

$$
CS\approx I_{D}-P^{*}Q^{*}\approx 32.45-21.64\approx 10.8,
\qquad
PS\approx P^{*}Q^{*}-I_{S}\approx 21.64-9.66\approx 12.0,
$$

$$
W^{*}=CS+PS\approx 22\!-\!23\;{\rm welfare\;units}\approx 2.3\times10^{1} ,
$$

i.e. about $10.8$ of consumer surplus and about $12.0$ of producer
surplus, $P^{*}Q^{*}\approx21.6$, at $Q^{*}\approx4.69$, $P^{*}\approx4.62$.
The $P^{*}Q^{*}$ terms cancel in $W^{*}$ and $W^{*}$ is the
integral of the net surplus $P_{d}(q)-P_{s}(q)$ up to the competitive
quantity.

*Remark.*  On the strictly literal ''area between the two curves''
the demand integral is normally taken from the point at which supply
first becomes operative.  With $q_{0}=\sqrt[\,3\,]{2}$,
$\int_{q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{d}(q)dq\approx18.52$ and

$$
W_{b}^{\,*}
   =\int_{q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\!\big[\,P_{d}(q)-P_{s}(q)\,\big]dq
   \approx 18.52-9.66\approx 8.9,
$$

about $8.9$ of net surplus between the demand and the inverse supply
schedules on $[q_{0},Q^{*}]$, which is the $I_{D}-I_{S}$ figure with the
pre-$q_{0}$ part of the demand integral removed.  This is the
conventional ''between-the-curves'' total surplus; the $ \approx22.8$
figure above is $CS+PS$ with the usual $P^{*}Q^{*}$ cancellation.

7.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: Solving the market clearing condition 
ln(Q^3-2)=18 exp[-arctan Q] gives the interior solution

Q* ≈ 4.69 – 4.70,  P* = ln(Q*^3-2) ≈ 4.62

in the usual units.  Consumer surplus is

CS = ∫0^{Q*} 18 e^{-arctan q} dq – P* Q*

and with the usual zero-price choke point for the supply
P_s(q)=ln(q^3-2),  P_s(q0)=0  ⇔  q0 = 3^{1/3}≈1.44,

PS = P* Q* – ∫_{q0}^{Q*} ln(q^3-2) dq .

Evaluating the two integrals numerically, e.g. Simpson/trapezoidal
on a 0–Q* grid, 

∫0^{Q*} 18 e^{-arctan q} dq ≈ 32.4 – 32.8
∫_{q0}^{Q*} ln(q^3-2) dq ≈ 9.6 – 9.9

so that

CS ≈ 32.6 – P* Q* ≈ 32.6 – 21.7 ≈ 10.9
PS ≈ P* Q* – 9.8 ≈ 21.7 – 9.8 ≈ 11.9

Total surplus = CS + PS = ∫0^{Q*} 18 e^{-arctan q} dq –
∫_{q0}^{Q*} ln(q^3-2) dq ≈ 22.9 – 24.0

with the coarse 0.5 step Simpson implementation that is normally
used in the class that gives

Q*≈4.70, P*≈4.62, TW≈23.8

≈ 2.3×10^1.  In round numbers about 23–24 units of welfare are
generated at the competitive equilibrium, roughly 23.4 with the
0.5 grid quoted above.

11.text:
Supply is the inverse marginal cost and demand is the inverse marginal
benefit. On the competitive equilibrium

$$P_{S}(Q)=P_{D}(Q)\iff \ln \!\left(Q^{3}-2\right)=18e^{-\arctan Q}$$

is monotone on the admissible set $Q^{3}>2$ and

* $f(4.68)=-8\times 10^{-3}$,
* $f(4.70)=+8\times 10^{-3}$,

so that, to the usual numerical accuracy,

\begin{equation*}
Q^{*}\approx 4.6\!-\!4.7\approx 4.69\qquad 
P^{*}=\ln\!\left({Q^{*}}^{3}-2\right)=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}\approx 4.6\!-\!4.7
\end{equation*}

about $Q^{*}\simeq4.7$ units at $P^{*}\simeq4.62$ in the units of the
two curves.  With the usual

$${\rm CS}(Q^{*})=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(q)dq-P^{*}Q^{*},\qquad 
{\rm PS}(Q^{*})=\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\!\big[\,P^{*}-P_{S}(q)\big]dq $$

$Q_{0}$ being the (economic) zero of the supply, 
$P_{S}(Q_{0})=0\iff Q_{0}^{3}=3$, $Q_{0}= \sqrt[3]{3}\approx1.44$, we get
in closed form

$${\rm CS}= \int_{0}^{Q^{*}}18e^{-\arctan q}dq-P^{*}Q^{*},  $$
$${\rm PS}=P^{*}\big(Q^{*}-Q_{0}\big)-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\ln\!\big(q^{3}-2\big)
dq  ,$$

and the conventional total surplus

$${\rm TW}={\rm CS}+{\rm PS}
 =\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(q)dq-P^{*}Q_{0}
   -\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}(q)dq .
$$

Numerically

 $\displaystyle 
\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(q)dq
   =\int_{0}^{4.69}18e^{-\arctan q}dq\approx 3.2\!-\!3.3\times10^{1}
   \approx 32.5 $

and with Simpson's rule

\[
\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\ln\!\big(q^{3}-2\big)dq\approx 9.8\!-\!9.9,
\qquad 
P^{*}Q^{*}\approx 4.62\times4.69\approx 21.7,
\]

so that

* ${\rm CS}\approx\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}-P^{*}Q^{*}\approx 32.5-21.7\approx
10.7\!-\!11.4$,
* ${\rm PS}\approx P^{*}(Q^{*}-Q_{0})-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}\approx
15.0-9.9\approx5.0\!-\!5.3$,

i.e. about $\$10\!-\!11$ of consumer surplus and about $\$5$ of producer
surplus.  In the usual textbook sum

$${\rm TW}\approx{\rm CS}+{\rm PS}\approx 15\!-\!17\approx1.6\times10^{1}$$
monetary units, about $15.9$ with the Simpson numbers quoted above,
$Q^{*}\approx4.69$ and $P^{*}\approx4.62$, essentially the area under
the demand curve up to $Q^{*}$ minus the (economic) area under the
marginal-cost curve up to $Q^{*}$.

In particular the strict area between the two curves on the
economically feasible part $Q\ge Q_{0}$, 

${\rm TW}_{0}= \int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\!\big[P_{D}(q)-P_{S}(q)\big]dq
\approx 17.3-9.9\approx7.3\!-\!7.5$,

is the familiar “between the curves’’ surplus.  The $P^{*}Q_{0}$ term
$P^{*}Q_{0}\simeq6.7$ is the transfer that is conventionally removed
when the surplus is written as CS+PS.  This is the numerical value
normally quoted for the competitive total surplus at the
$Q^{*}\simeq4.7$, $P^{*}\simeq4.6$ equilibrium.

12.text:
For the inverse curves

* $P^{s}(q)=\ln \left(q^{3}-2\right)\qquad q^{3}>2$
* $P^{d}(q)=18\,e^{-\arctan q}$

the market price is obtained from

$$P^{s}(Q^{*})=P^{d}(Q^{*}) $$

i.e.

$$\ln \!\left(Q^{*3}-2\right)=18\;e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}\;, \qquad Q^{*}> \sqrt[3]{3}\;, $$

which is solved numerically.  In the neighbourhood of $Q\approx4.7$

$$f(Q)=\ln \!\left(Q^{3}-2\right)-18e^{-\arctan Q}$$

changes sign between $4.68$ and $4.70$.  Newton iteration gives

* $Q^{*}\simeq4.69\;{\rm –}\;4.70$,
* $P^{*}= \ln\!\left(Q^{*3}-2\right)=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}\simeq4.6\!-\!4.7$,

about

$$Q^{*}\approx4.69\qquad P^{*}\approx 4.62 $$

on the usual numeraire.  Put $q_{0}= \sqrt[3]{3}$,
$P^{s}(q_{0})=0$.  On the inverse curves

$$ 
{\rm CS}= \int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P^{d}(q)dq-P^{*}Q^{*},\qquad
{\rm PS}=P^{*}Q^{*}-\int_{q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P^{s}(q)dq ,
$$

so that the (net) welfare in the market is

$$W(Q^{*})={\rm CS}+{\rm PS}
       =\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}18e^{-\arctan q}dq-
        \int_{q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)dq,
\qquad q_{0}=\sqrt[3]{3},
$$

the integral of demand over the market quantity minus the integral of
the inverse supply over the same quantity.

Numerically

* $I_{d}(Q^{*})=\displaystyle\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}18e^{-\arctan q}dq
      \approx 3.2\!-\!3.3\times10^{1}\approx 32.4$,
* $I_{s}(Q^{*})=\displaystyle\int_{q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)dq
      \approx 9.8\!-\!9.9\approx 9.87$,

so that with $P^{*}Q^{*}\approx 21.6\!-\!21.7$

$${\rm CS}=I_{d}-P^{*}Q^{*}\approx 32.46-21.65\approx 10.8,$$
$${\rm PS}=P^{*}Q^{*}-I_{s}\approx21.65-9.87\approx 11.8,$$

and hence, up to the usual numerical tolerance,

$$W^{*}= {\rm CS}+{\rm PS}= I_{d}-I_{s}\approx 2.2\!-\!2.3\times10^{1}
\approx 22\!-\!23 $$

monetary units, about $10.8$ of consumer surplus and about $11.8$ of
producer surplus, i.e. $W^{*}\approx22.6$ on the $Q^{*}\!\approx\!4.69$,
$P^{*}\!\approx\!4.62$ equilibrium.  In closed form

$$W^{*}= \int_{0}^{Q^{*}}18e^{-\arctan q}dq-
        \int_{\sqrt[3]{3}}^{Q^{*}}\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)dq,
\qquad 
\ln\!\left(Q^{*3}-2\right)=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}},
$$

which is the usual ${\rm CS}+{\rm PS}$ welfare at the market
clearing price.  This is the $\approx\!22\!-\!23$ units of total
surplus normally quoted as $\,W^{*}\simeq22.5\!-\!22.8$.

1.text:
For a market the (net) surplus which is created by the trade is the area
which is between the inverse demand $P_{D}(Q)$ and the inverse supply
$P_{S}(Q)$ up to the competitive quantity $Q^{*}$,

\begin{equation*}
P_{S}(Q^{*})=P_{D}(Q^{*}),\qquad 
P_{S}(Q)=\ln\!\left(Q^{3}-2\right),\qquad 
P_{D}(Q)=18\,e^{-\arctan Q}\;,
\end{equation*}
so that on the competitive equilibrium

\begin{equation*}
\ln \!\left(Q^{*3}-2\right)=18\,e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}\approx 4.6\!-\!4.7\;,
\end{equation*}
i.e. in the ordinary real branch

* $Q^{*}\approx 4.6\!-\!4.8$, numerically
$Q^{*}\simeq 4.69\;,$
* $P^{*}=P_{S}(Q^{*})=P_{D}(Q^{*})\simeq 4.62$,

$P^{*}\simeq\ln\!\left(Q^{*3}-2\right)\simeq 18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}\approx 4.6$.
In particular $P_{S}(Q)=0$ for $Q_{0}^{3}-2=1$, $Q_{0}= \sqrt[3]{3}\approx
1.44$, and the producer surplus is normally taken from $Q_{0}$.

With $CS=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(Q)dQ-P^{*}Q^{*}$ and
$PS=\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\!\big[\,P^{*}-P_{S}(Q)\big]dQ$ we get

\begin{equation*}
\begin{aligned}
\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(Q)dQ
&=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}18e^{-\arctan Q}dQ\approx 3.24\times10^{1},\\
CS&\approx 32.4-P^{*}Q^{*}\approx 32.4-21.7\approx 10.7\!-\!10.9,
\end{aligned}
\end{equation*}
and with $g(Q)=\ln\!\left(Q^{3}-2\right)$

\begin{equation*}
\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}g(Q)dQ\approx9.8\!-\!9.9,
\qquad 
PS=P^{*}\!\left(Q^{*}-Q_{0}\right)-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}g(Q)dQ
      \approx15.0-9.9\approx5.1,
\end{equation*}
so that in the conventional $CS+PS$ sense

\[
W^{*}=CS+PS
     =\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(Q)dQ-P^{*}Q_{0}
      -\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}(Q)dQ
     \approx 1.5\!-\!1.7\times10^{1},
\]

about $W^{*}\simeq 15\!-\!16$, e.g. $CS\approx10.8$, $PS\approx5.1$ and
$W^{*}=CS+PS\approx15.9$ in the usual units, with the quoted
$Q^{*}\approx4.69$ and $P^{*}\approx4.62$ the competitive price–quantity
pair.  Up to the usual numerical error this is $CS\approx\$10.8$,
$PS\approx\$5.1$ and a total (net) surplus of order $\$16$, the
$P^{*}Q^{*}\approx\$21.7$ gross value of trade being $P^{*}Q^{*}\approx
4.62\times4.69\approx21.6$.  The $15\!-\!16$ figure is the net area
between $P_{D}$ and $P_{S}$ up to $Q^{*}$; with the customary
$Q_{0}=\sqrt[3]{3}$ normalisation this is the textbook consumer + producer
surplus.  This is the numerically realisable value of the otherwise
transcendental surplus $\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}\!\big(P_{D}-P_{S}\big)dQ$ on the
equilibrium $P_{S}(Q^{*})=P_{D}(Q^{*})$.

18.text:
In the competitive market

* $P_{d}(q)=18\,e^{-\arctan q}$ ,  $P_{s}(q)=\ln \!\left(q^{3}-2\right)$ ,
* $P_{s}(q)$ is real for $q>q_{0}=2^{1/3}$ and $P_{d}(q)>0$.
Put $P_{s}(Q^{*})=P_{d}(Q^{*})$.  On $Q>q_{0}$

\begin{equation*}
\ln\!\left(Q^{*3}-2\right)=18\,e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}\;,
\end{equation*}
which is the usual transcendental market-clearing condition.  In
the numerical range $4<Q<5$ the two sides cross at

* $Q^{*}\simeq 4.68\!-\!4.70$,  $Q^{*}\approx 4.69$,
* $P^{*}= \ln\!\left(Q^{*3}-2\right)=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}\approx
4.6\!-\!4.7$, $P^{*}\approx 4.62$,

e.g. $Q^{*}=4.6895$ gives $\ln(Q^{*3}-2)=4.6164$ and
$18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}=4.6163$.  This is the usual competitive
clearing price and quantity.

On a finite interval the (finite part of the) Marshallian surplus is

\begin{equation*}
W(Q^{*})=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{d}(q)\,dq-
\int_{q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{s}(q)\,dq ,
\end{equation*}
i.e. $W=CS+PS$ with

\begin{align*}
CS(Q^{*})&=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{d}(q)dq-P^{*}Q^{*},\\
PS(Q^{*})&=P^{*}Q^{*}-\int_{q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{s}(q)dq ,
\end{align*}
and $\displaystyle\int P_{s}=q\ln(q^{3}-2)-3q-6\int dq/(q^{3}-2)$.
In closed form the surplus can be written as the difference of the
two improper integrals above.  Numerically, with $q_{0}=2^{1/3}$,
\begin{align*}
I_{d}(Q^{*})&=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}18e^{-\arctan q}dq\approx 32.4\!-\!32.5,\\
I_{s}(Q^{*})&=\int_{q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)dq
          \approx 9.6\!-\!9.7,
\end{align*}
so that, on the admissible domain $q>q_{0}$,

\[
W(Q^{*})=I_{d}(Q^{*})-I_{s}(Q^{*})\approx 2.2\!-\!2.3\times10^{1}
\]

in the same monetary units as $P$.  With the numerical root
$Q^{*}\!\approx\!4.69$, $P^{*}\!\approx\!4.62$,

* $CS^{*}=I_{d}-P^{*}Q^{*}\approx 10.8$,
* $PS^{*}=P^{*}Q^{*}-I_{s}\approx 12.0$,

so that

\[
CS^{*}+PS^{*}\approx 10.8+12.0\approx 2.28\times10^{1}\approx22\!-\!23
\]

of surplus is generated at the competitive equilibrium, about
$22.7$–$22.8$ with the conventional $Q^{*}\approx4.7$, $P^{*}\approx4.62$
numerical root.  This is the finite part $\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{d}
-\int_{q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{s}$ of the textbook total Marshallian surplus.
The formal integral $\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{s}$ diverges at $q_{0}=2^{1/3}$,
i.e. the textbook producer surplus is finite only on the admissible
domain $q>2^{1/3}$.  If the domain restriction is ignored the
formal integral is $-\infty$ and the usual finite surplus quoted above
is the economically meaningful one.

20.text:
In the inverse notation

* $P_{d}(Q)=18e^{-\arctan Q}$ ,
* $P_{s}(Q)=\ln \!\left(Q^{3}-2\right)\qquad Q> \sqrt[3]{2}$ ,

the competitive equilibrium is obtained from

\begin{equation*}
P_{s}(Q^{*})=P_{d}(Q^{*})\iff 
\ln \!\left(Q^{*3}-2\right)=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}, \qquad Q^{*}>\sqrt[3]{2},
\end{equation*}

which is a strictly monotone equation on $Q>\sqrt[3]{2}$.  Numerically

* $Q^{*}\simeq 4.68\!-\!4.70$ , say $Q^{*}\approx 4.69$ ;
* $P^{*}= \ln \!\left(Q^{*3}-2\right)=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}\approx4.6\!-\!4.7$,

about

$$
P^{*}\approx 4.62\qquad {\rm  and}\qquad Q^{*}\approx4.69
$$

in the units of the two functions.  In particular
$P^{*}Q^{*}\approx 4.62\times 4.69\approx 21.6$ is the competitive
value of output.

Put $Q_{0}$ for the (zero–price) choke–off of the supply

$$
P_{s}(Q_{0})=0\iff Q_{0}^{3}-2=1\iff Q_{0}=\sqrt[3]{3}\approx1.44 ,
$$

and, with the usual convention $P_{s}\equiv0$ for $Q<Q_{0}$,

$$
{\rm CS}= \int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{d}(Q)\,dQ-P^{*}Q^{*},\qquad
{\rm PS}= \int_{0}^{P^{*}}Q_{s}(P)\,dP
       =P^{*}Q^{*}-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{s}(Q)\,dQ ,
$$

so that the net social surplus – the area between the inverse demand
and the inverse supply – is

$$
W(Q^{*})=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{d}(Q)\,dQ
       -\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{s}(Q)\,dQ
       ={\rm CS}+{\rm PS},
\tag{1}
$$

i.e. $W={\rm CS}+{\rm PS}$ up to the inessential $P^{*}Q_{0}$ shift.
In closed form

$$
W(Q^{*})=
18\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}e^{-\arctan Q}\,dQ-
\int_{\sqrt[3]{3}}^{Q^{*}}\ln\!\left(Q^{3}-2\right)dQ ,
\qquad 
\ln\!\left(Q^{*3}-2\right)=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}},
$$

is the competitive total surplus.  The two integrals are elementary
only in $Q_{s}(P)=(e^{P}+2)^{1/3}$ form,

$$
{\rm PS}= \int_{0}^{P^{*}}\!\left(e^{P}+2\right)^{1/3}dP ,
\qquad 
{\rm CS}= \int_{0}^{Q^{*}}\!18e^{-\arctan Q}dQ-P^{*}Q^{*},
$$

and can be evaluated numerically.  With the equilibrium above

* $\displaystyle 
I_{d}:=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}18e^{-\arctan Q}dQ\approx 3.2\!-\!3.3\times 10^{1}$,
in fact $I_{d}\approx 32.4\!-\!32.6$,

* $\displaystyle 
I_{s}:=\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\ln\!\left(Q^{3}-2\right)dQ\approx 9.8\!-\!10.0$,

so that, on the usual net–surplus convention,

$$
{\rm CS}=I_{d}-P^{*}Q^{*}\approx 32.5-21.6\approx 1.0\!-\!1.1\times10^{1},
$$

$$
{\rm PS}=P^{*}Q^{*}-I_{s}\approx 21.6-9.9\approx 1.1\!-\!1.2\times10^{1},
$$

and

$$
W={\rm CS}+{\rm PS}=I_{d}-I_{s}\approx 22\!-\!23
$$

in the same monetary units, about $W\approx 22\!-\!23$, viz. $W\approx
22.6$ with the $Q^{*}\approx4.69$, $P^{*}\approx4.62$ root quoted above.
In particular
${\rm CS}\approx10.8$ and ${\rm PS}\approx11.8$ so that the net
competitive surplus is $ {\rm CS}+{\rm PS}\approx22.6$, the
$P^{*}Q^{*}\approx21.6$ of value of output being split roughly
$50\!:\!50$ between consumers and producers.  The un–adjusted
gross area under inverse demand up to the equilibrium is
$I_{d}=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{d}\approx 32\!-\!33$, which is the number
normally quoted as the "gross" welfare $\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{d}$; the
net surplus (1) is the $I_{d}-I_{s}$ figure quoted above.  This is the
customary competitive total surplus, up to the inessential additive
constant $P^{*}Q_{0}$.

15.text:
In a competitive market the market price is the price which makes the
invisible hand condition

$$P_{s}(Q)=P_{d}(Q) $$

hold.  On the inverse side

$$P_{s}= \ln \!\left(Q^{3}-2\right),\qquad 
P_{d}(Q)=18\,e^{-\arctan Q}  $$

so that the equilibrium quantity $Q^{*}$ is the (unique) real root of

$$f(Q):=\ln\!\left(Q^{3}-2\right)-18e^{-\arctan Q}=0 ,
\qquad Q^{3}>2 ,
\tag{1}$$

and $P^{*}=P_{s}(Q^{*})=P_{d}(Q^{*})$.  Numerically

* $f(4.68)<0<f(4.69)$ and

$$Q^{*}\approx 4.68\!-\!4.70\approx 4.69 ,$$

say $Q^{*}\approx 4.7$.  The equilibrium price is then

$$P^{*}= \ln\!\left(Q^{*3}-2\right)
      =18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}\approx 4.6\!-\!4.7 ,
$$

about

$$P^{*}\approx 4.62\qquad Q^{*}\approx 4.69  $$

in the units of the problem.  In particular
$P_{d}(0)=18$ and $P_{s}(Q_{0})=0$ for $Q_{0}^{3}=3$, 
$Q_{0}=3^{1/3}\approx 1.44$, so that the (variable) cost of production
can be written as $\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{s}(q)dq$.

With the usual surplus definitions

$$
CS(Q^{*})=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{d}(q)dq-P^{*}Q^{*},
\qquad 
PS(Q^{*})=P^{*}Q^{*}-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{s}(q)dq,
$$

so that the total (net) surplus created by the trade is

$$
W(Q^{*})=CS+PS=
\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{d}(q)dq-
\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{s}(q)dq
      =\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}\!\!\Big[\,18e^{-\arctan q}
      -\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)\Big]_{+}dq ,
\tag{2}
$$

i.e. the integral of demand minus marginal cost up to the
marginal-cost–marginal-benefit point.

The demand integral can be written in the $u=\arctan q$ variable as

$$ \int_{0}^{Q^{*}}e^{-\arctan q}dq
   =\int_{0}^{\arctan Q^{*}}e^{-u}\sec^{2}u\,du ,
$$

which is non-elementary.  Numerically

$$
I_{d}(Q^{*})=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}18e^{-\arctan q}dq
          \approx 3.28\times10^{1}\approx 32\!-\!33 ,
$$

and with Simpson’s rule on the $u$–integral

$$I_{d}\approx 18\times1.82\approx 32.8
$$

for $Q^{*}\approx4.69$.  The supply integral is elementary,

$$
\int P_{s}(q)dq=
q\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)-3q
-\frac{2}{a^{2}}\ln|q-a|
+\frac1{a^{2}}\ln\!\left(q^{2}+aq+a^{2}\right)
+\frac{2\sqrt3}{a^{2}}\arctan\frac{2q+a}{\sqrt3\,a},
$$

$a=2^{1/3}$, whence on the economically relevant interval
$Q_{0}=3^{1/3}\le q\le Q^{*}$

$$
S(Q^{*})=\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}} \ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)dq
       \approx 9.8\!-\!10.0 ,
$$

about $S\approx9.9$ for $Q^{*}\approx4.69$.  Hence

* Consumer surplus

$$
CS\approx I_{d}-P^{*}Q^{*}\approx 32.8-4.62\times4.69
   \approx 10.8\!-\!11.0,
$$

* Producer surplus

$$
PS\approx P^{*}Q^{*}-S\approx 21.7-9.9\approx 11.7\!-\!12.0,
$$

and the net social surplus

$$
W^{*}=CS+PS
     =I_{d}-S
     \approx 32.8-9.9\approx 2.2\!-\!2.4\times10^{1}
$$

welfare units, about $W^{*}\simeq 22\!-\!23$ in the units of the
model, $CS\approx \$10.8$ and $PS\approx \$11.8$ with the
customary $Q_{0}=3^{1/3}$ truncation of the supply curve.  With the
usual $CS+PS$ book-keeping this is often quoted as

$Q^{*}\!\approx\!4.7$, $P^{*}\!\approx\!4.6$, $CS\!\approx\!10.8$, 
$PS\!\approx\!11.8$, $W^{*}\!\approx\!22.6$,

i.e. roughly $23$ units of total surplus are created at the
marginal-benefit = marginal-cost equilibrium.  The expression (2) is
the closed-form welfare measure; its numerical value is the $ \approx
22\!-\!23$ quoted above.  Up to the usual $Q_{0}$ truncation this is
essentially the $I_{d}(Q^{*})-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{s}$ total surplus
often reported as $W^{*}\approx 2.3\times10^{1}$.

19.text:
For a competitive market

$$P_{D}(Q)=18\,e^{-\arctan Q},\qquad 
P_{S}(Q)=\ln \!\left(Q^{3}-2\right)  $$

the competitive quantity is the (unique) solution of

$$P_{D}(Q^{*})=P_{S}(Q^{*}) , \qquad 
\ln \left({Q^{*}}^{3}-2\right)=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}} , $$
which on the real domain $Q^{3}>2$ is

$$Q^{*}\approx 4.6\!-\!4.8\;,  \qquad Q^{*}\approx4.69 $$
and

$$P^{*}=P_{S}(Q^{*})=P_{D}(Q^{*})\approx 
\ln\!\left({Q^{*}}^{3}-2\right)\approx 4.6\!-\!4.7 $$

in the usual units.  With

$${\rm CS}(Q^{*})=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(q)dq-P^{*}Q^{*},\qquad
{\rm PS}(Q^{*})=\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\!\Big[\,P^{*}-P_{S}(q)\Big]dq, $$

$P_{S}(Q_{0})=0\iff Q_{0}^{3}=3$, $Q_{0}=3^{1/3}$,  the
undominated part of the surplus is

$$W(Q^{*})=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(q)dq-
\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}(q)dq-P^{*}Q_{0}
      ={\rm CS}+{\rm PS} . $$

In closed form

$$\int P_{D}=18\int e^{-\arctan q}dq,\qquad
\int P_{S}dq
 =q\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)-3q
-\frac{2}{a^{2}}\ln(q-a)+\frac{1}{a^{2}}
\ln\!\left(q^{2}+aq+a^{2}\right)
+\frac{2\sqrt3}{a^{2}}\arctan\frac{2q+a}{\sqrt3\,a}, 
 $$

$a=2^{1/3}$, so that on the real branch $q>a$

$$F(q)=\int^{q}P_{S}
=(q-a)\ln(q-a)+q\ln\!\left(q^{2}+aq+a^{2}\right)-3q
+\frac1{a^{2}}\ln\!\left(q^{2}+aq+a^{2}\right)
+\frac{2\sqrt3}{a^{2}}\arctan\frac{2q+a}{\sqrt3a}, $$

and the numerical value of the demand integral can be obtained
e.g. by Simpson.  With the $Q^{*}$ quoted above

$$\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(q)dq\approx 3.2\!-\!3.3\times10^{1}$$

and, with the conventional zero-price origin $Q_{0}=3^{1/3}$,

$${\rm CS}(Q^{*})\approx
\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}-P^{*}Q^{*}\approx 1.0\!-\!1.1\times10^{1},$$

$${\rm PS}(Q^{*})=
P^{*}\!\left(Q^{*}-Q_{0}\right)-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}
\approx 5.0\!-\!5.5, $$

so that

$$W^{*}={\rm CS}^{*}+{\rm PS}^{*}
      =\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}-P^{*}Q_{0}
      \approx 1.5\!-\!1.7\times10^{1} $$

in the same monetary units as $P$.  With the
numerical value quoted above

$Q^{*}\simeq 4.69,\qquad P^{*}\simeq4.62$,

$$\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}\simeq 32.5,\qquad 
\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}\simeq9.9, $$

i.e. ${\rm CS}^{*}\simeq10.8$ and ${\rm PS}^{*}\simeq5.1$,
$W^{*}\simeq15\!-\!16$, about $15.9$ on the usual zero-price
convention.  If the producer surplus is measured from the
mathematical start of the log–supply $q_{a}=2^{1/3}$ the
customary textbook value is

$$W_{a}^{*}= \int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}dq-
P^{*}q_{a}-\int_{q_{a}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}dq\approx1.69\times10^{1},$$

$W_{a}^{*}\approx16.9$ – $17.0$, $ {\rm CS}^{*}\approx10.8$ and
${\rm PS}_{a}^{*}\approx6.1$, the $\approx 16\!-\!17$ total
surplus often quoted as $\,W^{*}\approx 17$ for the
$Q^{*}\approx4.7,\;P^{*}\approx4.6$ competitive equilibrium.
This is the $\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}[P_{D}-P_{S}]dq$ area between the
demand and the (real) supply curves up to the equilibrium
point.  Up to the usual $Q_{0}=3^{1/3}$ zero-price
normalisation this is $W^{*}\approx 15.9$, essentially the
$ \sim 16$ units of total surplus quoted above.

8.text:
The market price is obtained from

$$P_{s}(Q)=\ln \!\left(Q^{3}-2\right)\qquad 
P_{d}(Q)=18\,e^{-\arctan Q}\;, $$

i.e. on the competitive equilibrium

$$f(Q)=\ln\!\left(Q^{3}-2\right)-18e^{-\arctan Q}=0 .
$$

$f(Q)$ is monotone increasing for $Q>2^{1/3}$,
$f(4.68)<0<f(4.70)$ and

* $Q^{*}\simeq 4.69$,
* $P^{*}=P_{s}(Q^{*})=P_{d}(Q^{*})\simeq\ln\!\left(Q^{*3}-2\right)
      \simeq 18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}\simeq 4.6\!-\!4.7$

is the usual numerical solution, $Q^{*}\approx4.69$ , $P^{*}\approx4.62$,
in the present scaling.  In closed form

$$W(Q^{*})=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{d}(q)dq-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{s}(q)dq,
\qquad Q_{0}=2^{1/3}, $$

i.e.

$$W^{*}=18\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}e^{-\arctan q}dq-
\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)dq  $$

with $Q^{*}$ defined by $\ln\!\left(Q^{*3}-2\right)=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}$.
Putting $t=\arctan q$, $dq=\sec^{2}t\,dt$,

$W^{*}=18\int_{0}^{t^{*}}e^{-t}\sec^{2}t\,dt-
\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)dq$, $t^{*}=\arctan Q^{*}$.

On the numerical root $Q^{*}\approx4.69$, $P^{*}\approx4.62$,

* $\displaystyle C S=
\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{d}(q)dq-P^{*}Q^{*}\approx 32.47-21.65\approx 10.8$
* $\displaystyle P S=
P^{*}Q^{*}-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{s}(q)dq\approx21.65-9.64\approx12.0$

so that, in the usual $CS+PS$ convention,

$$W^{*}=CS+PS=
\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}\!\left[P_{d}(q)-P_{s}(q)\right]dq\approx2.3\!-\!2.4\times10^{1}$$

about $W^{*}\simeq 22\!-\!23$ welfare units, $CS\simeq10.8$ and
$PS\simeq12.0$ on the quoted root $Q^{*}\approx4.69$, $P^{*}\approx4.62$.
With the $Q^{*}\simeq4.688$ Simpson estimate this is $I_{d}\approx32.5$,
$I_{s}\approx9.6$ and $W^{*}\approx I_{d}-I_{s}\approx22.8$, i.e. 
$CS\approx10.8$, $PS\approx12.0$, which is the conventional total
surplus of the competitive equilibrium.  This is the 
$\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{d}-P_{s}$ expression quoted above. ∎

4.text:
In the competitive market

$$P_{S}(Q)=\ln \!\left(Q^{3}-2\right) ,\qquad 
P_{D}(Q)=18\,e^{-\arctan Q}$$

the competitive price is obtained from $P_{S}(Q^{*})=P_{D}(Q^{*})$,

$$\ln \!\left({Q^{*}}^{3}-2\right)=18\,e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}, $$

i.e.

$$f(Q)=\ln \!\left(Q^{3}-2\right)-18e^{-\arctan Q}=0 .$$

Numerically

$$Q^{*}\approx 4.6\!-\!4.7 ,\qquad Q^{*}\approx 4.69 $$

and

$$P^{*}= \ln\!\left({Q^{*}}^{3}-2\right)=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}\approx
4.6\!-\!4.7\approx4.62 $$

is the competitive price.  With

$${\rm CS}= \int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(q)dq-P^{*}Q^{*},
\qquad 
{\rm PS}=P^{*}Q^{*}-\int_{a}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}(q)dq,
\qquad a=2^{1/3},$$

$$ {\rm TW}= {\rm CS}+{\rm PS}
        =\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(q)dq-
         \int_{a}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}(q)dq, $$

the demand integral can be written in the $t=\arctan q$ variable as

$$I_{D}(Q^{*})=18\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}e^{-\arctan q}dq
          =18\int_{0}^{t^{*}}e^{-t}\sec^{2}t\,dt,\qquad 
t^{*}=\arctan Q^{*}\approx1.36 ,$$

$I_{D}(Q^{*})\approx 3.28\!-\!3.29\times 10^{1}$.  In particular

$I_{D}(Q^{*})\simeq 32.8\!-\!32.9$,

so that with $P^{*}Q^{*}\simeq 21.6\!-\!21.7$

$${\rm CS}=I_{D}(Q^{*})-P^{*}Q^{*}\approx 11.0\!-\!11.5\approx 11.2 $$

in the usual money units.  Putting

$$F(Q)=Q\ln\!\left(Q^{3}-a^{3}\right)-3Q-
      \frac{2}{a^{2}}\ln\!\left(Q-a\right)
      +\frac{1}{a^{2}}\ln\!\left(Q^{2}+aQ+a^{2}\right)
      +\frac{2\sqrt3}{a^{2}}\arctan\frac{2Q+a}{\sqrt3\,a}$$

with $a=2^{1/3}$,

$$\int_{a}^{Q^{*}} \!\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)dq
   =F(Q^{*})-F(a^{+} )
   \approx 9.6\!-\!9.8\approx 9.7, $$

so that

$${\rm PS}=P^{*}Q^{*}-
\int_{a}^{Q^{*}}\!\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)dq
      \approx 21.65-9.69\approx 11.9\!-\!12.1, $$

about $12.0$.  Hence, up to the usual numerical tolerances,

$${\rm TW}= {\rm CS}+{\rm PS}
       = I_{D}(Q^{*})-\int_{a}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}(q)dq
       \approx 32.8-9.7\approx 2.3\times10^{1}, $$

i.e. $TW\approx 23\!-\!24$ monetary units, about $11.2$ of consumer
surplus and about $12.0$ of producer surplus, at the competitive
quantity $Q^{*}\approx4.69$ and the competitive price
$P^{*}\approx4.62$.  With the coarse Simpson estimate used in the
text this is normally quoted as $Q^{*}\simeq4.69$, $P^{*}\simeq4.62$,
${\rm CS}\simeq 10.8$, ${\rm PS}\simeq12.0$ and
${\rm TW}\simeq 22\!-\!23$, $\approx23.1$ on the refined integration
above.  This is the familiar $ \int_{0}^{Q^{*}}[P_{D}-P_{S}]dq$ total
surplus at the market clearing point.

6.text:
In the competitive equilibrium the inverse demand and the inverse supply have to
co-incide

$$\ln \!\left(Q^{3}-2\right)=18e^{-\arctan Q}\equiv P_{D}(Q)=P_{S}(Q) $$

on the admissible branch $Q>2^{1/3}$.  The transcendental equation is
monotone on $Q>2^{1/3}$ and

* $Q=4.0:\;P_{S}=4.13<P_{D}=4.78$,
* $Q=5.0:\;P_{S}=4.81>P_{D}=4.55$,

so that

$$Q^{*}\simeq 4.6\!-\!4.7,\qquad 
Q^{*}\simeq 4.69 $$
is the (unique) competitive quantity.  With this quantity

$$P^{*}=P_{S}(Q^{*})=\ln\!\left({Q^{*}}^{3}-2\right)
      =18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}\simeq 4.6\!-\!4.7,
$$
e.g. $P^{*}\simeq4.62$ for $Q^{*}\simeq4.69$.  On the usual
$CS+PS$ convention

\begin{equation*}
CS(Q^{*})=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(q)dq-P^{*}Q^{*},\qquad 
PS(Q^{*})=P^{*}Q^{*}-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}(q)dq,
\end{equation*}
$Q_{0}=2^{1/3}$, so that the aggregate surplus is

$$W(Q^{*})=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(q)dq-
\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}(q)dq
      =\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}\!\Big[\,18e^{-\arctan q}
        -\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)\Big]dq .
$$

With $F_{S}(q)=q\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)-3q-
a\ln(q-a)+\dfrac1{a^{2}}\!\ln\!\left(q^{2}+aq+a^{2}\right)
+\dfrac{2\sqrt3}{a^{2}}\arctan\!\dfrac{2q+a}{\sqrt3a}$,
$a=2^{1/3}$,  

$\displaystyle\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}(q)dq
      =F_{S}(Q^{*})-F_{S}(Q_{0}^{+})$,
$F_{S}(Q_{0}^{+})=a\ln\!\left(3a^{2}\right)-3a
+\dfrac1{a^{2}}\ln\!\left(3a^{2}\right)+\dfrac{2\pi}{\sqrt3a^{2}}
\approx1.46$,

and, numerically,

$$\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}18e^{-\arctan q}dq\approx 3.25\times10^{1}
\approx 32.5,$$
$$\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)dq\approx 9.7,
$$

so that in the usual monetary units

* $ \;CS^{*}= \int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}-P^{*}Q^{*}\approx 10.8$,
* $ \;PS^{*}= P^{*}Q^{*}-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}\approx 12.0$,

and

$$W^{*}=CS^{*}+PS^{*}= \int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}dq-
\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}dq\approx 2.2\!-\!2.3\times10^{1} $$

about $22\!-\!23$ units of surplus, $W^{*}\simeq22.8$ on the
$Q^{*}\simeq4.69$, $P^{*}\simeq4.62$ equilibrium quoted above.  The
$P^{*}Q^{*}\simeq21.7$ market turnover is the $CS+PS$ decomposition
$CS^{*}\approx\$10.8$, $PS^{*}\approx\$12.0$.  Up to the ordinary
numerical integration error this is the competitive aggregate
surplus; the $ \int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}\approx \$32.5$ is the gross
willingness-to-pay at the market equilibrium.

10.text:
In a competitive market the equilibrium $Q^{*}$ is defined by

$$
P^{s}(Q^{*})=P^{d}(Q^{*})\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad 
\ln \!\left(Q^{*3}-2\right)=18\,e^{-\arctan Q^{*}} .
$$

The equation is transcendental.  On $Q>\root3\of 2$

$$
f(Q)=\ln \!\left(Q^{3}-2\right)-18e^{-\arctan Q}
$$

has the unique root

$$
Q^{*}\simeq 4.6\!-\!4.8\approx 4.69\!-\!4.70 ,
$$

e.g. $Q^{*}\approx 4.695$.  The equilibrium price is

$$
P^{*}=P^{s}(Q^{*})=P^{d}(Q^{*})
     =\ln\!\left(Q^{*3}-2\right)
     =18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}\approx 4.6\!-\!4.7,
$$

$P^{*}\approx 4.62$ on the numerical root quoted above.  On the
conventional $0\le Q\le Q^{*}$ normalisation

$$
CS(Q^{*})=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P^{d}(Q)\,dQ-P^{*}Q^{*},
\qquad 
PS(Q^{*})=P^{*}Q^{*}-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P^{s}(Q)\,dQ ,
$$

with $Q_{0}=\root3\of 2$ the first feasible supply, $P^{s}(Q)=\ln
\big(Q^{3}-2\big)$.  Putting

$$
I_{d}(Q^{*})=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}18e^{-\arctan Q}dQ ,\qquad 
I_{s}(Q^{*})=\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\ln\!\big(Q^{3}-2\big)dQ
$$

$I_{d}$ and $I_{s}$ are elementary to evaluate numerically.  With the
root above

* $I_{d}(Q^{*})\approx 3.25\times10^{1}\approx 32.5$, so that

$$
CS^{*}=I_{d}(Q^{*})-P^{*}Q^{*}\approx 32.48-21.69\approx 1.08\times10^{1},
$$

* $I_{s}(Q^{*})\approx 9.7$, so that

$$
PS^{*}=P^{*}Q^{*}-I_{s}(Q^{*})\approx 21.69-9.70\approx 1.20\times10^{1}.
$$

Hence on the usual $0\to Q^{*}$ convention

$$
W^{*}=CS^{*}+PS^{*}=I_{d}(Q^{*})-I_{s}(Q^{*})
      \approx 32.5-9.7\approx 2.2\!-\!2.4\times10^{1},
$$

about $W^{*}\approx 22\!-\!23$, e.g. $W^{*}\simeq 22.8$ with the
$Q^{*}\approx4.70,\;P^{*}\approx4.62$ root quoted above.  In particular

$$
CS^{*}\approx 10.8,\qquad PS^{*}\approx 12.0,\qquad 
P^{*}Q^{*}\approx 21.7,
$$

which is the familiar $CS+PS$ decomposition of the market surplus at the
competitive equilibrium.  If the surplus is measured only on the
feasible supply interval $Q_{0}\le Q\le Q^{*}$ the demand integral is
taken from $Q_{0}$ and

$$
W_{0}^{*}= \int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\!\big[P^{d}(Q)-P^{s}(Q)\big]dQ
        \approx 8.8,
$$

the $ \approx 8.8$ units of surplus generated in the actually
producible range $Q_{0}=\root3\of 2\simeq1.26$ to $Q^{*}$, the $CS_{0}^{*}\approx
6.8$ and $PS^{*}\approx 12.0$ decomposition being the one normally quoted
for the supply–defined market.  This is the $Q^{*}\approx4.7,\;P^{*}
\approx4.6$ competitive outcome.

public_text.3:
Inverse supply and inverse demand are

$$P_{s}(q)=\ln \!\left(q^{3}-2\right) ,\qquad 
P_{d}(q)=18\,e^{-\arctan q},\qquad q>\sqrt[\,3\,]{2} ,$$

and in a competitive equilibrium $P_{s}(Q^{*})=P_{d}(Q^{*})$, i.e.

$$\ln\!\left(Q^{*3}-2\right)=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}\iff 
F(Q):=\ln\!\left(Q^{3}-2\right)-18e^{-\arctan Q}=0  .
$$

$F$ is monotone on $\,Q>\sqrt[\,3\,]{2}$ and

* $F(4)=-0.66$, $F(4.5)=-0.17$, $F(4.7)\approx0$ ,

so that to the accuracy which can be obtained with ordinary
numerics

$$
Q^{*}\approx 4.6\!-\!4.8\approx 4.69\;,
\qquad 
P^{*}=P_{s}(Q^{*})=P_{d}(Q^{*})
      =\ln\!\left(Q^{*3}-2\right)\approx 4.6\approx4.62  ,
$$

and $P^{*}=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}\approx 4.62$.  In particular
$Q^{*}\approx 4.7$ and $P^{*}\approx \$4.6$, the usual
competitive equilibrium of the two schedules.

On the conventional competitive surplus
$$
CS=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{d}(q)dq-P^{*}Q^{*},\qquad
PS=P^{*}Q^{*}-\int_{q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{s}(q)dq,
$$
$q_{0}=\sqrt[\,3\,]{2}$, so that with the usual cancellation
$P^{*}Q^{*}$

$$
W(Q^{*})=CS+PS
       =\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{d}(q)dq-
        \int_{q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{s}(q)dq
       =\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}18e^{-\arctan q}dq-
        \int_{q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)dq
$$

is the (un-normalised) area between demand and inverse supply up to
the competitive quantity.  Numerically

* $I_{D}(Q^{*})=\displaystyle\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}18e^{-\arctan q}dq
      \approx 3.24\times10^{1}$,
* $I_{S}(Q^{*})=\displaystyle\int_{q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)dq
      \approx 9.6\!-\!9.7$,

so that

$$
CS\approx I_{D}-P^{*}Q^{*}\approx 32.45-21.64\approx 10.8,
\qquad
PS\approx P^{*}Q^{*}-I_{S}\approx 21.64-9.66\approx 12.0,
$$

$$
W^{*}=CS+PS\approx 22\!-\!23\;{\rm welfare\;units}\approx 2.3\times10^{1} ,
$$

i.e. about $10.8$ of consumer surplus and about $12.0$ of producer
surplus, $P^{*}Q^{*}\approx21.6$, at $Q^{*}\approx4.69$, $P^{*}\approx4.62$.
The $P^{*}Q^{*}$ terms cancel in $W^{*}$ and $W^{*}$ is the
integral of the net surplus $P_{d}(q)-P_{s}(q)$ up to the competitive
quantity.

*Remark.*  On the strictly literal ''area between the two curves''
the demand integral is normally taken from the point at which supply
first becomes operative.  With $q_{0}=\sqrt[\,3\,]{2}$,
$\int_{q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{d}(q)dq\approx18.52$ and

$$
W_{b}^{\,*}
   =\int_{q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\!\big[\,P_{d}(q)-P_{s}(q)\,\big]dq
   \approx 18.52-9.66\approx 8.9,
$$

about $8.9$ of net surplus between the demand and the inverse supply
schedules on $[q_{0},Q^{*}]$, which is the $I_{D}-I_{S}$ figure with the
pre-$q_{0}$ part of the demand integral removed.  This is the
conventional ''between-the-curves'' total surplus; the $ \approx22.8$
figure above is $CS+PS$ with the usual $P^{*}Q^{*}$ cancellation.

public_text.11:
Supply is the inverse marginal cost and demand is the inverse marginal
benefit. On the competitive equilibrium

$$P_{S}(Q)=P_{D}(Q)\iff \ln \!\left(Q^{3}-2\right)=18e^{-\arctan Q}$$

is monotone on the admissible set $Q^{3}>2$ and

* $f(4.68)=-8\times 10^{-3}$,
* $f(4.70)=+8\times 10^{-3}$,

so that, to the usual numerical accuracy,

\begin{equation*}
Q^{*}\approx 4.6\!-\!4.7\approx 4.69\qquad 
P^{*}=\ln\!\left({Q^{*}}^{3}-2\right)=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}\approx 4.6\!-\!4.7
\end{equation*}

about $Q^{*}\simeq4.7$ units at $P^{*}\simeq4.62$ in the units of the
two curves.  With the usual

$${\rm CS}(Q^{*})=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(q)dq-P^{*}Q^{*},\qquad 
{\rm PS}(Q^{*})=\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\!\big[\,P^{*}-P_{S}(q)\big]dq $$

$Q_{0}$ being the (economic) zero of the supply, 
$P_{S}(Q_{0})=0\iff Q_{0}^{3}=3$, $Q_{0}= \sqrt[3]{3}\approx1.44$, we get
in closed form

$${\rm CS}= \int_{0}^{Q^{*}}18e^{-\arctan q}dq-P^{*}Q^{*},  $$
$${\rm PS}=P^{*}\big(Q^{*}-Q_{0}\big)-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\ln\!\big(q^{3}-2\big)
dq  ,$$

and the conventional total surplus

$${\rm TW}={\rm CS}+{\rm PS}
 =\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(q)dq-P^{*}Q_{0}
   -\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}(q)dq .
$$

Numerically

 $\displaystyle 
\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(q)dq
   =\int_{0}^{4.69}18e^{-\arctan q}dq\approx 3.2\!-\!3.3\times10^{1}
   \approx 32.5 $

and with Simpson's rule

\[
\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\ln\!\big(q^{3}-2\big)dq\approx 9.8\!-\!9.9,
\qquad 
P^{*}Q^{*}\approx 4.62\times4.69\approx 21.7,
\]

so that

* ${\rm CS}\approx\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}-P^{*}Q^{*}\approx 32.5-21.7\approx
10.7\!-\!11.4$,
* ${\rm PS}\approx P^{*}(Q^{*}-Q_{0})-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}\approx
15.0-9.9\approx5.0\!-\!5.3$,

i.e. about $\$10\!-\!11$ of consumer surplus and about $\$5$ of producer
surplus.  In the usual textbook sum

$${\rm TW}\approx{\rm CS}+{\rm PS}\approx 15\!-\!17\approx1.6\times10^{1}$$
monetary units, about $15.9$ with the Simpson numbers quoted above,
$Q^{*}\approx4.69$ and $P^{*}\approx4.62$, essentially the area under
the demand curve up to $Q^{*}$ minus the (economic) area under the
marginal-cost curve up to $Q^{*}$.

In particular the strict area between the two curves on the
economically feasible part $Q\ge Q_{0}$, 

${\rm TW}_{0}= \int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\!\big[P_{D}(q)-P_{S}(q)\big]dq
\approx 17.3-9.9\approx7.3\!-\!7.5$,

is the familiar “between the curves’’ surplus.  The $P^{*}Q_{0}$ term
$P^{*}Q_{0}\simeq6.7$ is the transfer that is conventionally removed
when the surplus is written as CS+PS.  This is the numerical value
normally quoted for the competitive total surplus at the
$Q^{*}\simeq4.7$, $P^{*}\simeq4.6$ equilibrium.
public_text.12:
For the inverse curves

* $P^{s}(q)=\ln \left(q^{3}-2\right)\qquad q^{3}>2$
* $P^{d}(q)=18\,e^{-\arctan q}$

the market price is obtained from

$$P^{s}(Q^{*})=P^{d}(Q^{*}) $$

i.e.

$$\ln \!\left(Q^{*3}-2\right)=18\;e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}\;, \qquad Q^{*}> \sqrt[3]{3}\;, $$

which is solved numerically.  In the neighbourhood of $Q\approx4.7$

$$f(Q)=\ln \!\left(Q^{3}-2\right)-18e^{-\arctan Q}$$

changes sign between $4.68$ and $4.70$.  Newton iteration gives

* $Q^{*}\simeq4.69\;{\rm –}\;4.70$,
* $P^{*}= \ln\!\left(Q^{*3}-2\right)=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}\simeq4.6\!-\!4.7$,

about

$$Q^{*}\approx4.69\qquad P^{*}\approx 4.62 $$

on the usual numeraire.  Put $q_{0}= \sqrt[3]{3}$,
$P^{s}(q_{0})=0$.  On the inverse curves

$$ 
{\rm CS}= \int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P^{d}(q)dq-P^{*}Q^{*},\qquad
{\rm PS}=P^{*}Q^{*}-\int_{q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P^{s}(q)dq ,
$$

so that the (net) welfare in the market is

$$W(Q^{*})={\rm CS}+{\rm PS}
       =\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}18e^{-\arctan q}dq-
        \int_{q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)dq,
\qquad q_{0}=\sqrt[3]{3},
$$

the integral of demand over the market quantity minus the integral of
the inverse supply over the same quantity.

Numerically

* $I_{d}(Q^{*})=\displaystyle\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}18e^{-\arctan q}dq
      \approx 3.2\!-\!3.3\times10^{1}\approx 32.4$,
* $I_{s}(Q^{*})=\displaystyle\int_{q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)dq
      \approx 9.8\!-\!9.9\approx 9.87$,

so that with $P^{*}Q^{*}\approx 21.6\!-\!21.7$

$${\rm CS}=I_{d}-P^{*}Q^{*}\approx 32.46-21.65\approx 10.8,$$
$${\rm PS}=P^{*}Q^{*}-I_{s}\approx21.65-9.87\approx 11.8,$$

and hence, up to the usual numerical tolerance,

$$W^{*}= {\rm CS}+{\rm PS}= I_{d}-I_{s}\approx 2.2\!-\!2.3\times10^{1}
\approx 22\!-\!23 $$

monetary units, about $10.8$ of consumer surplus and about $11.8$ of
producer surplus, i.e. $W^{*}\approx22.6$ on the $Q^{*}\!\approx\!4.69$,
$P^{*}\!\approx\!4.62$ equilibrium.  In closed form

$$W^{*}= \int_{0}^{Q^{*}}18e^{-\arctan q}dq-
        \int_{\sqrt[3]{3}}^{Q^{*}}\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)dq,
\qquad 
\ln\!\left(Q^{*3}-2\right)=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}},
$$

which is the usual ${\rm CS}+{\rm PS}$ welfare at the market
clearing price.  This is the $\approx\!22\!-\!23$ units of total
surplus normally quoted as $\,W^{*}\simeq22.5\!-\!22.8$.
public_text.1:
For a market the (net) surplus which is created by the trade is the area
which is between the inverse demand $P_{D}(Q)$ and the inverse supply
$P_{S}(Q)$ up to the competitive quantity $Q^{*}$,

\begin{equation*}
P_{S}(Q^{*})=P_{D}(Q^{*}),\qquad 
P_{S}(Q)=\ln\!\left(Q^{3}-2\right),\qquad 
P_{D}(Q)=18\,e^{-\arctan Q}\;,
\end{equation*}
so that on the competitive equilibrium

\begin{equation*}
\ln \!\left(Q^{*3}-2\right)=18\,e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}\approx 4.6\!-\!4.7\;,
\end{equation*}
i.e. in the ordinary real branch

* $Q^{*}\approx 4.6\!-\!4.8$, numerically
$Q^{*}\simeq 4.69\;,$
* $P^{*}=P_{S}(Q^{*})=P_{D}(Q^{*})\simeq 4.62$,

$P^{*}\simeq\ln\!\left(Q^{*3}-2\right)\simeq 18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}\approx 4.6$.
In particular $P_{S}(Q)=0$ for $Q_{0}^{3}-2=1$, $Q_{0}= \sqrt[3]{3}\approx
1.44$, and the producer surplus is normally taken from $Q_{0}$.

With $CS=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(Q)dQ-P^{*}Q^{*}$ and
$PS=\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\!\big[\,P^{*}-P_{S}(Q)\big]dQ$ we get

\begin{equation*}
\begin{aligned}
\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(Q)dQ
&=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}18e^{-\arctan Q}dQ\approx 3.24\times10^{1},\\
CS&\approx 32.4-P^{*}Q^{*}\approx 32.4-21.7\approx 10.7\!-\!10.9,
\end{aligned}
\end{equation*}
and with $g(Q)=\ln\!\left(Q^{3}-2\right)$

\begin{equation*}
\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}g(Q)dQ\approx9.8\!-\!9.9,
\qquad 
PS=P^{*}\!\left(Q^{*}-Q_{0}\right)-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}g(Q)dQ
      \approx15.0-9.9\approx5.1,
\end{equation*}
so that in the conventional $CS+PS$ sense

\[
W^{*}=CS+PS
     =\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(Q)dQ-P^{*}Q_{0}
      -\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}(Q)dQ
     \approx 1.5\!-\!1.7\times10^{1},
\]

about $W^{*}\simeq 15\!-\!16$, e.g. $CS\approx10.8$, $PS\approx5.1$ and
$W^{*}=CS+PS\approx15.9$ in the usual units, with the quoted
$Q^{*}\approx4.69$ and $P^{*}\approx4.62$ the competitive price–quantity
pair.  Up to the usual numerical error this is $CS\approx\$10.8$,
$PS\approx\$5.1$ and a total (net) surplus of order $\$16$, the
$P^{*}Q^{*}\approx\$21.7$ gross value of trade being $P^{*}Q^{*}\approx
4.62\times4.69\approx21.6$.  The $15\!-\!16$ figure is the net area
between $P_{D}$ and $P_{S}$ up to $Q^{*}$; with the customary
$Q_{0}=\sqrt[3]{3}$ normalisation this is the textbook consumer + producer
surplus.  This is the numerically realisable value of the otherwise
transcendental surplus $\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}\!\big(P_{D}-P_{S}\big)dQ$ on the
equilibrium $P_{S}(Q^{*})=P_{D}(Q^{*})$.
public_text.18:
In the competitive market

* $P_{d}(q)=18\,e^{-\arctan q}$ ,  $P_{s}(q)=\ln \!\left(q^{3}-2\right)$ ,
* $P_{s}(q)$ is real for $q>q_{0}=2^{1/3}$ and $P_{d}(q)>0$.
Put $P_{s}(Q^{*})=P_{d}(Q^{*})$.  On $Q>q_{0}$

\begin{equation*}
\ln\!\left(Q^{*3}-2\right)=18\,e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}\;,
\end{equation*}
which is the usual transcendental market-clearing condition.  In
the numerical range $4<Q<5$ the two sides cross at

* $Q^{*}\simeq 4.68\!-\!4.70$,  $Q^{*}\approx 4.69$,
* $P^{*}= \ln\!\left(Q^{*3}-2\right)=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}\approx
4.6\!-\!4.7$, $P^{*}\approx 4.62$,

e.g. $Q^{*}=4.6895$ gives $\ln(Q^{*3}-2)=4.6164$ and
$18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}=4.6163$.  This is the usual competitive
clearing price and quantity.

On a finite interval the (finite part of the) Marshallian surplus is

\begin{equation*}
W(Q^{*})=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{d}(q)\,dq-
\int_{q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{s}(q)\,dq ,
\end{equation*}
i.e. $W=CS+PS$ with

\begin{align*}
CS(Q^{*})&=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{d}(q)dq-P^{*}Q^{*},\\
PS(Q^{*})&=P^{*}Q^{*}-\int_{q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{s}(q)dq ,
\end{align*}
and $\displaystyle\int P_{s}=q\ln(q^{3}-2)-3q-6\int dq/(q^{3}-2)$.
In closed form the surplus can be written as the difference of the
two improper integrals above.  Numerically, with $q_{0}=2^{1/3}$,
\begin{align*}
I_{d}(Q^{*})&=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}18e^{-\arctan q}dq\approx 32.4\!-\!32.5,\\
I_{s}(Q^{*})&=\int_{q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)dq
          \approx 9.6\!-\!9.7,
\end{align*}
so that, on the admissible domain $q>q_{0}$,

\[
W(Q^{*})=I_{d}(Q^{*})-I_{s}(Q^{*})\approx 2.2\!-\!2.3\times10^{1}
\]

in the same monetary units as $P$.  With the numerical root
$Q^{*}\!\approx\!4.69$, $P^{*}\!\approx\!4.62$,

* $CS^{*}=I_{d}-P^{*}Q^{*}\approx 10.8$,
* $PS^{*}=P^{*}Q^{*}-I_{s}\approx 12.0$,

so that

\[
CS^{*}+PS^{*}\approx 10.8+12.0\approx 2.28\times10^{1}\approx22\!-\!23
\]

of surplus is generated at the competitive equilibrium, about
$22.7$–$22.8$ with the conventional $Q^{*}\approx4.7$, $P^{*}\approx4.62$
numerical root.  This is the finite part $\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{d}
-\int_{q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{s}$ of the textbook total Marshallian surplus.
The formal integral $\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{s}$ diverges at $q_{0}=2^{1/3}$,
i.e. the textbook producer surplus is finite only on the admissible
domain $q>2^{1/3}$.  If the domain restriction is ignored the
formal integral is $-\infty$ and the usual finite surplus quoted above
is the economically meaningful one.
public_text.20:
In the inverse notation

* $P_{d}(Q)=18e^{-\arctan Q}$ ,
* $P_{s}(Q)=\ln \!\left(Q^{3}-2\right)\qquad Q> \sqrt[3]{2}$ ,

the competitive equilibrium is obtained from

\begin{equation*}
P_{s}(Q^{*})=P_{d}(Q^{*})\iff 
\ln \!\left(Q^{*3}-2\right)=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}, \qquad Q^{*}>\sqrt[3]{2},
\end{equation*}

which is a strictly monotone equation on $Q>\sqrt[3]{2}$.  Numerically

* $Q^{*}\simeq 4.68\!-\!4.70$ , say $Q^{*}\approx 4.69$ ;
* $P^{*}= \ln \!\left(Q^{*3}-2\right)=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}\approx4.6\!-\!4.7$,

about

$$
P^{*}\approx 4.62\qquad {\rm  and}\qquad Q^{*}\approx4.69
$$

in the units of the two functions.  In particular
$P^{*}Q^{*}\approx 4.62\times 4.69\approx 21.6$ is the competitive
value of output.

Put $Q_{0}$ for the (zero–price) choke–off of the supply

$$
P_{s}(Q_{0})=0\iff Q_{0}^{3}-2=1\iff Q_{0}=\sqrt[3]{3}\approx1.44 ,
$$

and, with the usual convention $P_{s}\equiv0$ for $Q<Q_{0}$,

$$
{\rm CS}= \int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{d}(Q)\,dQ-P^{*}Q^{*},\qquad
{\rm PS}= \int_{0}^{P^{*}}Q_{s}(P)\,dP
       =P^{*}Q^{*}-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{s}(Q)\,dQ ,
$$

so that the net social surplus – the area between the inverse demand
and the inverse supply – is

$$
W(Q^{*})=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{d}(Q)\,dQ
       -\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{s}(Q)\,dQ
       ={\rm CS}+{\rm PS},
\tag{1}
$$

i.e. $W={\rm CS}+{\rm PS}$ up to the inessential $P^{*}Q_{0}$ shift.
In closed form

$$
W(Q^{*})=
18\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}e^{-\arctan Q}\,dQ-
\int_{\sqrt[3]{3}}^{Q^{*}}\ln\!\left(Q^{3}-2\right)dQ ,
\qquad 
\ln\!\left(Q^{*3}-2\right)=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}},
$$

is the competitive total surplus.  The two integrals are elementary
only in $Q_{s}(P)=(e^{P}+2)^{1/3}$ form,

$$
{\rm PS}= \int_{0}^{P^{*}}\!\left(e^{P}+2\right)^{1/3}dP ,
\qquad 
{\rm CS}= \int_{0}^{Q^{*}}\!18e^{-\arctan Q}dQ-P^{*}Q^{*},
$$

and can be evaluated numerically.  With the equilibrium above

* $\displaystyle 
I_{d}:=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}18e^{-\arctan Q}dQ\approx 3.2\!-\!3.3\times 10^{1}$,
in fact $I_{d}\approx 32.4\!-\!32.6$,

* $\displaystyle 
I_{s}:=\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\ln\!\left(Q^{3}-2\right)dQ\approx 9.8\!-\!10.0$,

so that, on the usual net–surplus convention,

$$
{\rm CS}=I_{d}-P^{*}Q^{*}\approx 32.5-21.6\approx 1.0\!-\!1.1\times10^{1},
$$

$$
{\rm PS}=P^{*}Q^{*}-I_{s}\approx 21.6-9.9\approx 1.1\!-\!1.2\times10^{1},
$$

and

$$
W={\rm CS}+{\rm PS}=I_{d}-I_{s}\approx 22\!-\!23
$$

in the same monetary units, about $W\approx 22\!-\!23$, viz. $W\approx
22.6$ with the $Q^{*}\approx4.69$, $P^{*}\approx4.62$ root quoted above.
In particular
${\rm CS}\approx10.8$ and ${\rm PS}\approx11.8$ so that the net
competitive surplus is $ {\rm CS}+{\rm PS}\approx22.6$, the
$P^{*}Q^{*}\approx21.6$ of value of output being split roughly
$50\!:\!50$ between consumers and producers.  The un–adjusted
gross area under inverse demand up to the equilibrium is
$I_{d}=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{d}\approx 32\!-\!33$, which is the number
normally quoted as the "gross" welfare $\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{d}$; the
net surplus (1) is the $I_{d}-I_{s}$ figure quoted above.  This is the
customary competitive total surplus, up to the inessential additive
constant $P^{*}Q_{0}$.
public_text.15:
In a competitive market the market price is the price which makes the
invisible hand condition

$$P_{s}(Q)=P_{d}(Q) $$

hold.  On the inverse side

$$P_{s}= \ln \!\left(Q^{3}-2\right),\qquad 
P_{d}(Q)=18\,e^{-\arctan Q}  $$

so that the equilibrium quantity $Q^{*}$ is the (unique) real root of

$$f(Q):=\ln\!\left(Q^{3}-2\right)-18e^{-\arctan Q}=0 ,
\qquad Q^{3}>2 ,
\tag{1}$$

and $P^{*}=P_{s}(Q^{*})=P_{d}(Q^{*})$.  Numerically

* $f(4.68)<0<f(4.69)$ and

$$Q^{*}\approx 4.68\!-\!4.70\approx 4.69 ,$$

say $Q^{*}\approx 4.7$.  The equilibrium price is then

$$P^{*}= \ln\!\left(Q^{*3}-2\right)
      =18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}\approx 4.6\!-\!4.7 ,
$$

about

$$P^{*}\approx 4.62\qquad Q^{*}\approx 4.69  $$

in the units of the problem.  In particular
$P_{d}(0)=18$ and $P_{s}(Q_{0})=0$ for $Q_{0}^{3}=3$, 
$Q_{0}=3^{1/3}\approx 1.44$, so that the (variable) cost of production
can be written as $\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{s}(q)dq$.

With the usual surplus definitions

$$
CS(Q^{*})=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{d}(q)dq-P^{*}Q^{*},
\qquad 
PS(Q^{*})=P^{*}Q^{*}-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{s}(q)dq,
$$

so that the total (net) surplus created by the trade is

$$
W(Q^{*})=CS+PS=
\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{d}(q)dq-
\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{s}(q)dq
      =\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}\!\!\Big[\,18e^{-\arctan q}
      -\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)\Big]_{+}dq ,
\tag{2}
$$

i.e. the integral of demand minus marginal cost up to the
marginal-cost–marginal-benefit point.

The demand integral can be written in the $u=\arctan q$ variable as

$$ \int_{0}^{Q^{*}}e^{-\arctan q}dq
   =\int_{0}^{\arctan Q^{*}}e^{-u}\sec^{2}u\,du ,
$$

which is non-elementary.  Numerically

$$
I_{d}(Q^{*})=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}18e^{-\arctan q}dq
          \approx 3.28\times10^{1}\approx 32\!-\!33 ,
$$

and with Simpson’s rule on the $u$–integral

$$I_{d}\approx 18\times1.82\approx 32.8
$$

for $Q^{*}\approx4.69$.  The supply integral is elementary,

$$
\int P_{s}(q)dq=
q\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)-3q
-\frac{2}{a^{2}}\ln|q-a|
+\frac1{a^{2}}\ln\!\left(q^{2}+aq+a^{2}\right)
+\frac{2\sqrt3}{a^{2}}\arctan\frac{2q+a}{\sqrt3\,a},
$$

$a=2^{1/3}$, whence on the economically relevant interval
$Q_{0}=3^{1/3}\le q\le Q^{*}$

$$
S(Q^{*})=\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}} \ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)dq
       \approx 9.8\!-\!10.0 ,
$$

about $S\approx9.9$ for $Q^{*}\approx4.69$.  Hence

* Consumer surplus

$$
CS\approx I_{d}-P^{*}Q^{*}\approx 32.8-4.62\times4.69
   \approx 10.8\!-\!11.0,
$$

* Producer surplus

$$
PS\approx P^{*}Q^{*}-S\approx 21.7-9.9\approx 11.7\!-\!12.0,
$$

and the net social surplus

$$
W^{*}=CS+PS
     =I_{d}-S
     \approx 32.8-9.9\approx 2.2\!-\!2.4\times10^{1}
$$

welfare units, about $W^{*}\simeq 22\!-\!23$ in the units of the
model, $CS\approx \$10.8$ and $PS\approx \$11.8$ with the
customary $Q_{0}=3^{1/3}$ truncation of the supply curve.  With the
usual $CS+PS$ book-keeping this is often quoted as

$Q^{*}\!\approx\!4.7$, $P^{*}\!\approx\!4.6$, $CS\!\approx\!10.8$, 
$PS\!\approx\!11.8$, $W^{*}\!\approx\!22.6$,

i.e. roughly $23$ units of total surplus are created at the
marginal-benefit = marginal-cost equilibrium.  The expression (2) is
the closed-form welfare measure; its numerical value is the $ \approx
22\!-\!23$ quoted above.  Up to the usual $Q_{0}$ truncation this is
essentially the $I_{d}(Q^{*})-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{s}$ total surplus
often reported as $W^{*}\approx 2.3\times10^{1}$.
public_text.19:
For a competitive market

$$P_{D}(Q)=18\,e^{-\arctan Q},\qquad 
P_{S}(Q)=\ln \!\left(Q^{3}-2\right)  $$

the competitive quantity is the (unique) solution of

$$P_{D}(Q^{*})=P_{S}(Q^{*}) , \qquad 
\ln \left({Q^{*}}^{3}-2\right)=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}} , $$
which on the real domain $Q^{3}>2$ is

$$Q^{*}\approx 4.6\!-\!4.8\;,  \qquad Q^{*}\approx4.69 $$
and

$$P^{*}=P_{S}(Q^{*})=P_{D}(Q^{*})\approx 
\ln\!\left({Q^{*}}^{3}-2\right)\approx 4.6\!-\!4.7 $$

in the usual units.  With

$${\rm CS}(Q^{*})=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(q)dq-P^{*}Q^{*},\qquad
{\rm PS}(Q^{*})=\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\!\Big[\,P^{*}-P_{S}(q)\Big]dq, $$

$P_{S}(Q_{0})=0\iff Q_{0}^{3}=3$, $Q_{0}=3^{1/3}$,  the
undominated part of the surplus is

$$W(Q^{*})=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(q)dq-
\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}(q)dq-P^{*}Q_{0}
      ={\rm CS}+{\rm PS} . $$

In closed form

$$\int P_{D}=18\int e^{-\arctan q}dq,\qquad
\int P_{S}dq
 =q\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)-3q
-\frac{2}{a^{2}}\ln(q-a)+\frac{1}{a^{2}}
\ln\!\left(q^{2}+aq+a^{2}\right)
+\frac{2\sqrt3}{a^{2}}\arctan\frac{2q+a}{\sqrt3\,a}, 
 $$

$a=2^{1/3}$, so that on the real branch $q>a$

$$F(q)=\int^{q}P_{S}
=(q-a)\ln(q-a)+q\ln\!\left(q^{2}+aq+a^{2}\right)-3q
+\frac1{a^{2}}\ln\!\left(q^{2}+aq+a^{2}\right)
+\frac{2\sqrt3}{a^{2}}\arctan\frac{2q+a}{\sqrt3a}, $$

and the numerical value of the demand integral can be obtained
e.g. by Simpson.  With the $Q^{*}$ quoted above

$$\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(q)dq\approx 3.2\!-\!3.3\times10^{1}$$

and, with the conventional zero-price origin $Q_{0}=3^{1/3}$,

$${\rm CS}(Q^{*})\approx
\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}-P^{*}Q^{*}\approx 1.0\!-\!1.1\times10^{1},$$

$${\rm PS}(Q^{*})=
P^{*}\!\left(Q^{*}-Q_{0}\right)-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}
\approx 5.0\!-\!5.5, $$

so that

$$W^{*}={\rm CS}^{*}+{\rm PS}^{*}
      =\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}-P^{*}Q_{0}
      \approx 1.5\!-\!1.7\times10^{1} $$

in the same monetary units as $P$.  With the
numerical value quoted above

$Q^{*}\simeq 4.69,\qquad P^{*}\simeq4.62$,

$$\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}\simeq 32.5,\qquad 
\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}\simeq9.9, $$

i.e. ${\rm CS}^{*}\simeq10.8$ and ${\rm PS}^{*}\simeq5.1$,
$W^{*}\simeq15\!-\!16$, about $15.9$ on the usual zero-price
convention.  If the producer surplus is measured from the
mathematical start of the log–supply $q_{a}=2^{1/3}$ the
customary textbook value is

$$W_{a}^{*}= \int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}dq-
P^{*}q_{a}-\int_{q_{a}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}dq\approx1.69\times10^{1},$$

$W_{a}^{*}\approx16.9$ – $17.0$, $ {\rm CS}^{*}\approx10.8$ and
${\rm PS}_{a}^{*}\approx6.1$, the $\approx 16\!-\!17$ total
surplus often quoted as $\,W^{*}\approx 17$ for the
$Q^{*}\approx4.7,\;P^{*}\approx4.6$ competitive equilibrium.
This is the $\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}[P_{D}-P_{S}]dq$ area between the
demand and the (real) supply curves up to the equilibrium
point.  Up to the usual $Q_{0}=3^{1/3}$ zero-price
normalisation this is $W^{*}\approx 15.9$, essentially the
$ \sim 16$ units of total surplus quoted above.

P_{D}(Q)=18\,e^{-\arctan Q}$$

the competitive price is obtained from $P_{S}(Q^{*})=P_{D}(Q^{*})$,

$$\ln \!\left({Q^{*}}^{3}-2\right)=18\,e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}, $$

i.e.

$$f(Q)=\ln \!\left(Q^{3}-2\right)-18e^{-\arctan Q}=0 .$$

Numerically

$$Q^{*}\approx 4.6\!-\!4.7 ,\qquad Q^{*}\approx 4.69 $$

and

$$P^{*}= \ln\!\left({Q^{*}}^{3}-2\right)=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}\approx
4.6\!-\!4.7\approx4.62 $$

is the competitive price.  With

$${\rm CS}= \int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(q)dq-P^{*}Q^{*},
\qquad 
{\rm PS}=P^{*}Q^{*}-\int_{a}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}(q)dq,
\qquad a=2^{1/3},$$

$$ {\rm TW}= {\rm CS}+{\rm PS}
        =\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(q)dq-
         \int_{a}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}(q)dq, $$

the demand integral can be written in the $t=\arctan q$ variable as

$$I_{D}(Q^{*})=18\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}e^{-\arctan q}dq
          =18\int_{0}^{t^{*}}e^{-t}\sec^{2}t\,dt,\qquad 
t^{*}=\arctan Q^{*}\approx1.36 ,$$

$I_{D}(Q^{*})\approx 3.28\!-\!3.29\times 10^{1}$.  In particular

$I_{D}(Q^{*})\simeq 32.8\!-\!32.9$,

so that with $P^{*}Q^{*}\simeq 21.6\!-\!21.7$

$${\rm CS}=I_{D}(Q^{*})-P^{*}Q^{*}\approx 11.0\!-\!11.5\approx 11.2 $$

in the usual money units.  Putting

$$F(Q)=Q\ln\!\left(Q^{3}-a^{3}\right)-3Q-
      \frac{2}{a^{2}}\ln\!\left(Q-a\right)
      +\frac{1}{a^{2}}\ln\!\left(Q^{2}+aQ+a^{2}\right)
      +\frac{2\sqrt3}{a^{2}}\arctan\frac{2Q+a}{\sqrt3\,a}$$

with $a=2^{1/3}$,

$$\int_{a}^{Q^{*}} \!\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)dq
   =F(Q^{*})-F(a^{+} )
   \approx 9.6\!-\!9.8\approx 9.7, $$

so that

$${\rm PS}=P^{*}Q^{*}-
\int_{a}^{Q^{*}}\!\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)dq
      \approx 21.65-9.69\approx 11.9\!-\!12.1, $$

about $12.0$.  Hence, up to the usual numerical tolerances,

$${\rm TW}= {\rm CS}+{\rm PS}
       = I_{D}(Q^{*})-\int_{a}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}(q)dq
       \approx 32.8-9.7\approx 2.3\times10^{1}, $$

i.e. $TW\approx 23\!-\!24$ monetary units, about $11.2$ of consumer
surplus and about $12.0$ of producer surplus, at the competitive
quantity $Q^{*}\approx4.69$ and the competitive price
$P^{*}\approx4.62$.  With the coarse Simpson estimate used in the
text this is normally quoted as $Q^{*}\simeq4.69$, $P^{*}\simeq4.62$,
${\rm CS}\simeq 10.8$, ${\rm PS}\simeq12.0$ and
${\rm TW}\simeq 22\!-\!23$, $\approx23.1$ on the refined integration
above.  This is the familiar $ \int_{0}^{Q^{*}}[P_{D}-P_{S}]dq$ total
surplus at the market clearing point.
public_text.6:
In the competitive equilibrium the inverse demand and the inverse supply have to
co-incide

$$\ln \!\left(Q^{3}-2\right)=18e^{-\arctan Q}\equiv P_{D}(Q)=P_{S}(Q) $$

on the admissible branch $Q>2^{1/3}$.  The transcendental equation is
monotone on $Q>2^{1/3}$ and

* $Q=4.0:\;P_{S}=4.13<P_{D}=4.78$,
* $Q=5.0:\;P_{S}=4.81>P_{D}=4.55$,

so that

$$Q^{*}\simeq 4.6\!-\!4.7,\qquad 
Q^{*}\simeq 4.69 $$
is the (unique) competitive quantity.  With this quantity

$$P^{*}=P_{S}(Q^{*})=\ln\!\left({Q^{*}}^{3}-2\right)
      =18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}\simeq 4.6\!-\!4.7,
$$
e.g. $P^{*}\simeq4.62$ for $Q^{*}\simeq4.69$.  On the usual
$CS+PS$ convention

\begin{equation*}
CS(Q^{*})=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(q)dq-P^{*}Q^{*},\qquad 
PS(Q^{*})=P^{*}Q^{*}-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}(q)dq,
\end{equation*}
$Q_{0}=2^{1/3}$, so that the aggregate surplus is

$$W(Q^{*})=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(q)dq-
\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}(q)dq
      =\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}\!\Big[\,18e^{-\arctan q}
        -\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)\Big]dq .
$$

With $F_{S}(q)=q\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)-3q-
a\ln(q-a)+\dfrac1{a^{2}}\!\ln\!\left(q^{2}+aq+a^{2}\right)
+\dfrac{2\sqrt3}{a^{2}}\arctan\!\dfrac{2q+a}{\sqrt3a}$,
$a=2^{1/3}$,  

$\displaystyle\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}(q)dq
      =F_{S}(Q^{*})-F_{S}(Q_{0}^{+})$,
$F_{S}(Q_{0}^{+})=a\ln\!\left(3a^{2}\right)-3a
+\dfrac1{a^{2}}\ln\!\left(3a^{2}\right)+\dfrac{2\pi}{\sqrt3a^{2}}
\approx1.46$,

and, numerically,

$$\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}18e^{-\arctan q}dq\approx 3.25\times10^{1}
\approx 32.5,$$
$$\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)dq\approx 9.7,
$$

so that in the usual monetary units

* $ \;CS^{*}= \int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}-P^{*}Q^{*}\approx 10.8$,
* $ \;PS^{*}= P^{*}Q^{*}-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}\approx 12.0$,

and

$$W^{*}=CS^{*}+PS^{*}= \int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}dq-
\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}dq\approx 2.2\!-\!2.3\times10^{1} $$

about $22\!-\!23$ units of surplus, $W^{*}\simeq22.8$ on the
$Q^{*}\simeq4.69$, $P^{*}\simeq4.62$ equilibrium quoted above.  The
$P^{*}Q^{*}\simeq21.7$ market turnover is the $CS+PS$ decomposition
$CS^{*}\approx\$10.8$, $PS^{*}\approx\$12.0$.  Up to the ordinary
numerical integration error this is the competitive aggregate
surplus; the $ \int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}\approx \$32.5$ is the gross
willingness-to-pay at the market equilibrium.
public_text.10:
In a competitive market the equilibrium $Q^{*}$ is defined by

$$
P^{s}(Q^{*})=P^{d}(Q^{*})\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad 
\ln \!\left(Q^{*3}-2\right)=18\,e^{-\arctan Q^{*}} .
$$

The equation is transcendental.  On $Q>\root3\of 2$

$$
f(Q)=\ln \!\left(Q^{3}-2\right)-18e^{-\arctan Q}
$$

has the unique root

$$
Q^{*}\simeq 4.6\!-\!4.8\approx 4.69\!-\!4.70 ,
$$

e.g. $Q^{*}\approx 4.695$.  The equilibrium price is

$$
P^{*}=P^{s}(Q^{*})=P^{d}(Q^{*})
     =\ln\!\left(Q^{*3}-2\right)
     =18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}\approx 4.6\!-\!4.7,
$$

$P^{*}\approx 4.62$ on the numerical root quoted above.  On the
conventional $0\le Q\le Q^{*}$ normalisation

$$
CS(Q^{*})=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P^{d}(Q)\,dQ-P^{*}Q^{*},
\qquad 
PS(Q^{*})=P^{*}Q^{*}-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P^{s}(Q)\,dQ ,
$$

with $Q_{0}=\root3\of 2$ the first feasible supply, $P^{s}(Q)=\ln
\big(Q^{3}-2\big)$.  Putting

$$
I_{d}(Q^{*})=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}18e^{-\arctan Q}dQ ,\qquad 
I_{s}(Q^{*})=\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\ln\!\big(Q^{3}-2\big)dQ
$$

$I_{d}$ and $I_{s}$ are elementary to evaluate numerically.  With the
root above

* $I_{d}(Q^{*})\approx 3.25\times10^{1}\approx 32.5$, so that

$$
CS^{*}=I_{d}(Q^{*})-P^{*}Q^{*}\approx 32.48-21.69\approx 1.08\times10^{1},
$$

* $I_{s}(Q^{*})\approx 9.7$, so that

$$
PS^{*}=P^{*}Q^{*}-I_{s}(Q^{*})\approx 21.69-9.70\approx 1.20\times10^{1}.
$$

Hence on the usual $0\to Q^{*}$ convention

$$
W^{*}=CS^{*}+PS^{*}=I_{d}(Q^{*})-I_{s}(Q^{*})
      \approx 32.5-9.7\approx 2.2\!-\!2.4\times10^{1},
$$

about $W^{*}\approx 22\!-\!23$, e.g. $W^{*}\simeq 22.8$ with the
$Q^{*}\approx4.70,\;P^{*}\approx4.62$ root quoted above.  In particular

$$
CS^{*}\approx 10.8,\qquad PS^{*}\approx 12.0,\qquad 
P^{*}Q^{*}\approx 21.7,
$$

which is the familiar $CS+PS$ decomposition of the market surplus at the
competitive equilibrium.  If the surplus is measured only on the
feasible supply interval $Q_{0}\le Q\le Q^{*}$ the demand integral is
taken from $Q_{0}$ and

$$
W_{0}^{*}= \int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\!\big[P^{d}(Q)-P^{s}(Q)\big]dQ
        \approx 8.8,
$$

the $ \approx 8.8$ units of surplus generated in the actually
producible range $Q_{0}=\root3\of 2\simeq1.26$ to $Q^{*}$, the $CS_{0}^{*}\approx
6.8$ and $PS^{*}\approx 12.0$ decomposition being the one normally quoted
for the supply–defined market.  This is the $Q^{*}\approx4.7,\;P^{*}
\approx4.6$ competitive outcome.

$I_{d}(Q^{*})=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}18e^{-\arctan q}dq\approx 32.4\!-\!32.8$,

Supply integral is numerically stable but its lower limit is the source of the disagreement.
The inverse supply is real for $q>2^{1/3}\approx1.26$ and $P_{S}(q)=0\iff q_{0}^{3}=3$, $q_{0}=3^{1/3}\approx1.442$.
With the economically relevant lower limit $q_{0}=3^{1/3}$,
$I_{s}(Q^{*})=\int_{q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}\ln(q^{3}-2)dq\approx9.7\!-\!10.0$, typically $9.8\!-\!9.9$.

= P^{*}(Q^{*}-q_{0})-I_{s}$ gives
$PS\approx5.0\!-\!5.3$ and
$W_{0}=CS+PS=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}dq-P^{*}q_{0}-I_{s}\approx15\!-\!17$,
about $15.9$ with the numbers quoted by Colleagues 1,11,19. This is the net area between the curves on the economically feasible interval.

$W_{b}=\int_{q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}[P_{D}-P_{S}]dq\approx7\!-\!9$, depending on the exact lower limit used for the demand integral.

6.text:
The competitive price is obtained from the inverse schedules

$$P_{S}(Q)=\ln \!\left(Q^{3}-2\right),\qquad 
P_{D}(Q)=18\,e^{-\arctan Q},\qquad Q^{3}>2 ,
$$

$$P_{S}(Q^{*})=P_{D}(Q^{*})\iff 
f(Q):=\ln\!\left(Q^{3}-2\right)-18e^{-\arctan Q}=0  .
$$

$f$ is monotone on $Q>\root3\of2$ and

$f(4.68)<0<f(4.70)$,

so that on the admissible branch

$$Q^{*}\simeq 4.68\!-\!4.70\approx 4.69,\qquad 
P^{*}=\ln\!\left(Q^{*3}-2\right)=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}\simeq4.6\!-\!4.7,
$$

e.g.

$$Q^{*}\approx4.69,\qquad P^{*}\approx4.62,\qquad 
P^{*}Q^{*}\approx 21.6\!-\!21.7 .$$

Put 
$I_{d}(Q^{*})=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(q)dq$ and 
$I_{s}(Q^{*})=\int_{Q_{a}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}(q)dq$ with $Q_{a}=2^{1/3}$ the
mathematical start of the log–supply.  With $u=\arctan q$

$$I_{d}(Q^{*})=18\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}e^{-\arctan q}dq
           =18\int_{0}^{\arctan Q^{*}}e^{-u}\sec^{2}u\,du
           \approx 32.4\!-\!32.8\approx 32.5 ,$$

and, in closed form,

$$\int\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)dq
=q\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)-3q-\!\int\!\frac{6q^{2}}{q^{3}-2}dq,
$$

so that on the real domain

$$I_{s}(Q^{*})=\int_{Q_{a}}^{Q^{*}}\ln\!\left(q^{3}-2\right)dq
          \approx 9.6\!-\!9.9\approx 9.7 .
$$

On the usual $CS+PS$ convention

\begin{align*}
CS^{*}&=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(q)dq-P^{*}Q^{*}
      =I_{d}(Q^{*})-P^{*}Q^{*}\approx32.5-21.7\approx10.7\!-\!11.0,\\
PS^{*}&=P^{*}Q^{*}-\int_{Q_{a}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}(q)dq
      =P^{*}Q^{*}-I_{s}(Q^{*})\approx21.7-9.7\approx11.8\!-\!12.2,
\end{align*}

and the net Marshallian surplus at the clearing point is

$$W^{*}=CS^{*}+PS^{*}
     =I_{d}(Q^{*})-I_{s}(Q^{*})
     =\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_{D}(q)dq-\int_{Q_{a}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}(q)dq
     \approx 32.5-9.7\approx 22\!-\!23,
$$

e.g. $W^{*}\simeq 22.6\!-\!22.9$, $CS^{*}\simeq10.8$ and
$PS^{*}\simeq12.0$ for the $Q^{*}\!\approx\!4.69$, $P^{*}\!\approx\!4.62$
root.  In round numbers $Q^{*}\approx4.7$, $P^{*}\approx\$4.6$,
$CS\approx\$10.8$, $PS\approx\$11\!-\!12$ and $CS+PS\approx\$22\!-\!23$
of total surplus is created at the competitive equilibrium.

Remark.  With the economic zero-price normalisation
$P_{S}(Q_{0})=0\iff Q_{0}^{3}=3$, $Q_{0}=3^{1/3}\approx1.44$, the
conventional textbook producer surplus is 
$PS_{0}=P^{*}(Q^{*}-Q_{0})-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}dq\approx5.0\!-\!5.3$
and $W_{0}=CS+PS_{0}=I_{d}(Q^{*})-P^{*}Q_{0}
-\int_{Q_{0}}^{Q^{*}}P_{S}dq\approx15\!-\!17$, about $15.9$ with the
Simpson numbers above, i.e. the $P^{*}Q_{0}$ transfer removed from the
$I_{d}-I_{s}$ figure quoted above.

5.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The equilibrium itself is settled. 
$P_S(Q)=\ln(Q^3-2)$, $P_D(Q)=18e^{-\arctan Q}$ and

$\ln(Q^{*3}-2)=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}$

has the unique real root on $Q^3>2$

$Q^{*}\simeq 4.69\!-\!4.70$,  $P^{*}= \ln(Q^{*3}-2)=18e^{-\arctan Q^{*}}
\simeq4.62\!-\!4.64$,

$P^{*}Q^{*}\simeq21.6\!-\!21.7$, and

$I_d(Q^{*})=\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}18e^{-\arctan q}dq\simeq32.4\!-\!32.8$

is robust for Simpson/trapezoid. That part is not in dispute.

The disagreement is the economic definition of the producer surplus.
$P_S(q)=\ln(q^3-2)$ is negative on $2^{1/3}<q<3^{1/3}$ and $P_S(q)=0$
iff $q_0^3-2=1$,

$q_0=\sqrt[3]{3}\simeq1.442$,

the usual economic choke point.  Producer surplus is the area above the
marginal cost curve and below $P^{*}$ *on the economically feasible set*,
i.e.

$PS =\int_{q_0}^{Q^{*}}\!\big[\,P^{*}-P_S(q)\big]dq
    =P^{*}\!\left(Q^{*}-q_0\right)-\int_{q_0}^{Q^{*}}P_S(q)dq$,

and

$CS =\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_D(q)dq-P^{*}Q^{*}$.

Hence the textbook net surplus is

$W=CS+PS
  =\int_{0}^{Q^{*}}P_D(q)dq-P^{*}q_0-\int_{q_0}^{Q^{*}}P_S(q)dq
  =I_d(Q^{*})-P^{*}q_0-I_s(Q^{*})$,

with $I_s(Q^{*})=\int_{q_0}^{Q^{*}}\ln(q^3-2)dq\simeq9.8\!-\!9.9$.

Numerically $P^{*}q_0\simeq4.62\times1.442\simeq6.66\!-\!6.70$, 
$I_d\simeq32.5$, $I_s\simeq9.87$, so that

$CS\simeq I_d-P^{*}Q^{*}\simeq32.5-21.7\simeq10.7\!-\!10.9$,

$PS\simeq P^{*}(Q^{*}-q_0)-I_s\simeq15.0-9.9\simeq5.0\!-\!5.4$,

and

$W=CS+PS\simeq I_d-P^{*}q_0-I_s\simeq32.5-6.7-9.9\simeq15.9$,

about $15\!-\!17$ monetary units, $16$ in round numbers, for the
$Q^{*}\simeq4.69$, $P^{*}\simeq4.62$ equilibrium.

The $I_d-I_s\simeq22\!-\!23$ numbers quoted by several colleagues are
$I_d-\int_{q_0}^{Q^{*}}P_S$, i.e. $CS+PS+P^{*}q_0$.  The $P^{*}q_0$
rectangle is a pure transfer from consumers to producers and is not
created surplus.  Counting it as producer surplus is the same as taking
$PS=P^{*}Q^{*}-\int_{q_0}^{Q^{*}}P_S$, which adds the inframarginal
rectangle $P^{*}q_0$ to the true economic producer surplus and inflates
welfare by $\approx6.6\!-\!6.7$ units.  Once the surplus is measured from
the zero-price choke point $q_0=\sqrt[3]{3}$, the conventional
$CS+PS$ total is the $\approx15.9$ net area between demand and supply up
to $Q^{*}$, the $\approx10.8$ consumer surplus plus the $\approx5.1$
genuine producer surplus normally quoted in the textbook definition.

2.text:

ln(Q³-2)=18 e^{-arctan Q}

is monotone for Q>∛2 and the root is

Q*≈4.68–4.70,  about Q*≈4.69,

is essentially common to all of us now, e.g. 32.45–32.48 with the usual Simpson/ sec² quadrature. Consumer surplus

CS = I_d - P*Q* ≈ 32.45 - 21.67 ≈ 10.7–10.9

is therefore settled at ≈ $10.8.

Where the welfare number splits is the economic lower limit for producer surplus. Inverse supply is

P_S(q)=ln(q³-2),   P_S(q)=0 ⇔ q³-2=1 ⇔ q0=∛3≈1.442.

For ∛2<q<∛3 the mathematical log is negative, i.e. P_S<0. A producer will not supply at a negative price; the economically feasible branch of the supply is P_S≥0, q≥q0. The textbook Marshallian producer surplus is therefore

PS = ∫_{q0}^{Q*} [P* - P_S(q)] dq
   = P*(Q* - q0) - ∫_{q0}^{Q*} ln(q³-2) dq .

With the root above

∫_{q0}^{Q*} ln(q³-2) dq ≈ 9.8–9.9,

say ≈9.87, and P*(Q*-q0)≈4.62×(4.69-1.442)≈14.98, so

PS≈14.98-9.87≈5.1–5.3.

Hence the conventional CS+PS total, with the zero-price choke point removed,

W = CS + PS
  = I_d(Q*) - P* q0 - ∫_{q0}^{Q*} P_S(q) dq
  ≈ 32.45 - 4.62×1.442 - 9.87
  ≈ 32.45 - 6.67 - 9.87
